#456. World of Warcraft: Forever's in-game economy has been ravaged by an exploit that allowed players to farm thousands of gold

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (830 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

World of Warcraft: Forever's in-game economy has been ravaged by an exploit that allowed players to farm thousands of gold

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World of Warcraft: Forever has suffered its first economic nightmare, as a dungeon farm exploit has left some players with thousands of gold in their bags while the vast majority of players are barely above their first hundred.
  • Industry observers note that this exploit was swiftly and quietly hotfixed by Blizzard, but not before a right now-unknown number of players were able to make out like bandits.
  • It has been revealed that this was possible on every class, and according to Twitch streamer Ziqo, allowed players to farm out hundreds of gold in a few hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever has suffered its first economic nightmare, as a dungeon farm exploit has left some players with thousands of gold in their bags while the vast majority of players are barely above their first hundred.

Industry observers note that this exploit was swiftly and quietly hotfixed by Blizzard, but not before a right now-unknown number of players were able to make out like bandits. In basic terms, the new Blackmaw Hold dungeon includes several packs of non-elite, easy to kill enemies right at the start of the dungeon. Prior to the hotfix, the loot drop tables for these enemies were incorrect, and worth vastly more in terms of gold than they should have. Keen-eyed players spotted this but kept it quiet, running into the dungeon and quickly killing off these early mobs and resetting the dungeon every hour.

It has been revealed that this was possible on every class, and according to Twitch streamer Ziqo, allowed players to farm out hundreds of gold in a few hours. He is seen streaming with over 4,000 gold - and claims other streamers made out with more than that.

For an idea of how much money that is, one of the most expensive things a player will likely buy on their character throughout the original Classic World of Warcraft is the expert riding skill. It takes a long time to save up for, and stands as a major accomplishment in the life of a character. It costs around 900 gold. These players, in just a few days of dedicated grinding, will have been able to pay this price several times over.

Looking at community hubs for the game (Reddit or the official World of Warcraft forums), regular players are demanding Blizzard take action - going further than just the already-deployed hotfix. Maya on the WoW forum wants the ill-gotten gold to be removed and for players to be banned who made use of the Blackmaw Hold exploit, writing: "Remove the gold or I and many others will just quit. This is worse than the bots at this point.".

Flnrodi on Reddit, referring to streamers who took advantage of this exploit, wrote: "Not sure what to say. The fact that he did this all offstream claims enough that [Ziqo] (and others) knew that this is not intended and 100 percent considered an exploit. Personally, I think there should be some kind of punishment and definitely all the gold [should be] revoked.".

It has been revealed that you may be wondering why this is such a big deal? So what if a few players can get fancy mounts faster, or snatch up some really good gear on the player auction house? Well, exorbitant sums of money in the hands of a few players can have a massive impact on a server's economy. You could, for example, use your newfound wealth to flip every listing of a certain rare resource on the auction house and mark the price up significantly for profit, which obviously inflates the price for regular players. Likewise, you can out-bid other players for rare and powerful BOE items, which in turn raises the prices of those as sellers may find they can make more cash than they could off such drops prior to the exploit.

Industry observers note that this all has an inflationary effect, and could push a server's economy to a more expensive level faster than it otherwise would. Even if this effect isn't so drastic, these players can essentially gear out multiple characters in fantastic gear without putting in the hours, or out-bid the rest of the community on the Black Market Auction House for rare and largely unparalleled special loot.

Sources indicate that the counter argument against punitive measures is that these players didn't cheat. They didn't buy gold from real-money-traders, nor did they plug in some external tool to give them an unfair advantage over others. They simply put in the time to get to around level 55, ran a dungeon, and killed mobs repeatedly for valuable drops. Would it have been a good thing to flag the exploit the moment they found out about it? Sure. But once other players at your level take advantage of it, and no strict ruling around whether doing so is punishable, it's arguably in a player's best interest to join in while the going is good.

It has been revealed that as of writing, there's been no official word from Blizzard on what it intends to do beyond fixing the exploit. Given the required level to take on Blackmaw Hold, the number of exploiters cannot be too large, and the sheer amount of gold they gained in a small amount of time should make them easy to flag. Rolling back their accounts and reverting the gold they gained back to a pre-exploit amount certainly appears to be a popular option. Whether Blizzard actually does so, or enforces other punishments, is the major question.

#455. Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1335 w)

Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert.
  • It's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to.
  • I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert. It feels like the road has been erased, a sentence left unfinished. It's quietly strange, a weird bit of urban wrongfooting. But I guess it makes some kind of sense. California, after all, is home to California City, a town that was planned and then never really built. It sits out there now, north of Los Angeles, streets laid out but slowly being eaten by the sand and dirt. Still, 14,000 people lived there as of 2018. Design limitation or something stranger, this digital dead end is a reminder that all of this land, so modern, so ancient - all of this is spook country.

It's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to. As I've waited, like everyone else, for GTA 6, I've been back here in the GTA games of the past, via the slightly dodgy remasters from a few years ago. And what's come through for me, spending a few idle mornings messing around in San Andreas, a game I thought I knew pretty well, is how beautifully odd everything is now. The best part of 20 years have given a game that once strained against its host technology a genuine aesthetic. Surprisingly sparse in detailing, as angular and sheer as dream architecture, in love with expanses, San Andreas is perfectly placed, it seems to me, to capture just how weird California can be.

California and Nevada. This is the part I always forget. I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star. It has a bigger footprint than the earlier game, sure, but it uses that space to go deep on the detailing and the sense of a singular, fiercely specific place. San Andreas meanwhile offers three cities - and one of them isn't actually in California. Alongside spins on LA and San Francisco, you get a version of Las Vegas. It's quite neat really: the three points of some arcane spiritual triangle. The kind of thing Marvel Whiteside Parsons, aerospace engineer and Actual Wizard, might have scratched in the dust of his backyard to help him control the weather. He lived - and died - in Pasadena, so all this would have been familiar anyway.

Recent findings suggest that there is a classic moment in every GTA. A moment where the map opens up in the early games, or when you explore enough in the later games, and simply get to understand the audacity of what is being attempted here. In San Andreas, and this feels apt, the best way to have this moment is to break the rules, sneaking into the open map before the game is fully ready for you. An early mission allows you to step away from the critical path, as it were, and peg it to the airport in Los Santos, where a plane is waiting to be pinched. Taxi, feel the thrust, and you're off. LA beneath you - sorry, Los Santos - and on the horizon a dinkytown version of the Golden Gate Bridge and the MGM Grand.

Dinkytown is the word. From the sky, the huge map of San Andreas, which still feels like an incredible piece of work - such ambition! - can look like toys laid out on a duvet in the remasters. Coming back from GTA 5, a masterpiece of texture, the cities of San Andreas in particular feel very weird - cramped and condensed and wonderfully stagey, arranged the way a kid might jury-rig them together from shoeboxes and stray cardboard. On your way out of Grove Street early on you pass the Los Santos equivalent of the Hollywood sign, looming so close the way it does in the movies but not in the actual city and you feel you could touch it. Downtown is reduced to a handful of the best buildings - it's always pleasing to see the one from the brilliant first act of Speed made the cut - but still manages to capture the key stuff too, which in this case is the way that modern LA looms somewhat cruelly over the old city, captured with a strange sepulchral dignity in the form of the City Hall, so easy to spot but now so small!

Industry observers note that elsewhere, the ersatz Las Vega Strip looks like a drawing based on memory - a few of the classic shapes are there, but it's a sketch of a place. In this way, I guess, it captures a truth about Las Vegas. Also, perhaps, it's an admission that this is a town comfortably out of the reach of satire. As for San Francisco, it's a 60s cop movie delight to fishtail around. It nails the hills and what more do you need for a game with cars in it?

In a recent development, taken as a whole these cities feel mesmerising now. And it's the limitations that make them sing, I think: those sheer granite canyons of downtown LA with its towering blocks of architecture and surprisingly thin traffic, with only the very faintest of ambient soundtracks that ensures any gunfire will pop and clap and shake you out of your seat. (Remember, I am playing the remasters and sound effects may be missing.) This is the LA of Repo Man rather than Heat - an otherland where the buildings feel alien, even the air feels alien. At night, palm trees stand out against a sky that glows a deep, clean red. GTA 5 would finesse all of this, the skyboxes and whatnot, but perhaps in that finessing something is lost. (Both games, incidentally, have such a talent for capturing California's kitsch excess that they perhaps miss some of the sweeter truths, such as the astonishing diversity of cultures a city like Los Angeles finds homes for. But how could any game do that justice?).

In a recent development, dinkytowns aside, what San Andreas does better than GTA 5 is space - the peculiar flat spaces of Southern California in particular, a state in which you can never quite tell where the wilderness ends and the landscaping begins, and where the ancient rocks that announce the horizon can look new, like stage settings, while the freeways feel truly ancient, concrete lizards sleeping on the dirt, bleached by the easy sun. I can lose hours out here. I have had to double- and triple-check that GTA 5 is the bigger game, in fact, because San Andreas still feels absolutely enormous, a trick that works even when you can see the not-Golden Gate Bridge seconds after taking off from not-LAX. Grab a bike and you can spend an absolute age exploring the between-spaces which video game California and real California are both so good at conjuring, stumbling on little towns you will never stumble on again, passing commercial follies, listening as the radio pumps out "All My Exes Live in Texas".

It has been revealed that and, paradoxically, the more I play the more I realise San Andreas is very good at the little things in its own odd way. GTA 5 is an astonishing feat of seeing and transposing, but I don't think it has anything across its acres to match the sense of place offered by San Andreas' take on Grove Street, where the story begins. It's just a neighborhood, but as you cross its small space and recross it in the game's opening hours, learning how to eat food and buy clothes and get a haircut and spray paint on walls and all that jazz, the sense that this is your home is grooved and regrooved into the experience. Maybe this is why it's such a thrill to return to this earlier pass at Los Santos. Because this one is where you truly live.

#454. This AI knew the answers but didn’t understand the questions

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This AI knew the answers but didn’t understand the questions

📅 30 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Psychologists have long debated whether the human mind can be explained by a single, unified theory or if different functions such as attention and memory must be studied separately.
  • In July 2025, a study published in Nature introduced an AI model called "Centaur." Built on standard large language models and refined using data from psychological experiments, Centaur was designed to simulate human cognitive behavior.
  • A more recent study published in National Science Open challenges those claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Psychologists have long debated whether the human mind can be explained by a single, unified theory or if different functions such as attention and memory must be studied separately. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) is entering that debate, offering a latest way to explore how the mind works.

In July 2025, a study published in Nature introduced an AI model called "Centaur." Built on standard large language models and refined using data from psychological experiments, Centaur was designed to simulate human cognitive behavior. It reportedly performed well across 160 tasks, including decision-making, executive control, and other mental processes. The results drew widespread attention and were seen as a possible step toward AI systems that could replicate human thinking more broadly.

A more recent study published in National Science Open challenges those claims. Researchers from Zhejiang University argue that Centaur's apparent success may come from overfitting. In other words, instead of understanding the tasks, the model may have learned to recognize patterns in the training data and reproduce expected answers.

To test this idea, the researchers created several new evaluation scenarios. In one example, they replaced the original multiple-choice prompts, which described specific psychological tasks, with the instruction "Please choose option A." If the model truly understood the task, it should have consistently selected option A. Instead, Centaur continued to choose the "correct answers" from the original dataset.

It has been revealed that this behavior suggests that the model was not interpreting the meaning of the questions. Rather, it relied on learned statistical patterns to "guess" answers. The researchers compared this to a student who scores well by memorizing test formats without actually understanding the material.

Why This Matters for AI Evaluation.

According to recent reports, the findings highlight the need for caution when assessing the abilities of large language models. While these systems can be highly effective at fitting data, their "black-box" nature makes it difficult to know how they arrive at their outputs. This can lead to challenges such as hallucinations or misinterpretations. Careful and varied testing is essential to determine whether a model truly has the skills it appears to demonstrate.

The Real Challenge: Language Understanding.

Although Centaur was presented as a model capable of simulating cognition, its biggest limitation appears to be in language comprehension. Specifically, it struggles to recognize and respond to the intent behind questions. The study suggests that achieving true language understanding may be one of the most important challenges in developing AI systems that can model human cognition more fully.

Materials provided by Science China Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A high school in Canada has hit out at students for using food delivery services like Uber Eats and DoorDash to order “excessive” amounts of food during lessons.

If you’re too busy – or just feeling a little lazy – then it might be convenient for you to use a food delivery app to get some grub and much-needed supplies delivered to your door.

According to recent reports, however, school pupils are also using these services. As per CBC, one high school in Calgary has had to glitch a warning to parents over students’ use of the apps, with many taking time out of their classes to wait around for delivery drivers.

“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day,” St. Francis High School administrators said in a letter to parents.

According to CBC, the school officials noted that the deliveries might be “convenient” for students, but they also pose a “security risk” for the school as a whole.

They spoke to students who noted that some claim they need to use the bathroom, but then go wait outside for their delivery driver to meet them.

“Like if someone’s out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one’s allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” an 11th-grade student told CBC, who noted that some orders do get “excessive” at times.

High security prison investigating after inmate gets McDonald’s and alcohol delivered by drone.

School changes rules after student suspended for bringing coffee to class.

TikToker claims they were detained for delivering UberEats to Texas school.

According to recent reports, the report also stated that it is happening at elementary schools as well, with one school having a table set up for students to collect from. That one, however, is more a case of parents ordering for them.

CBC also noted that some delivery drivers have tried to pass food through class windows at other schools too.

It isn’t just a problem for schools in Canada, either. Back in mid-October, the nation’s most secure prison rolled out an investigation after inmates had been receiving McDonald’s and alcohol by drones.

Over in New York, a school was forced to change its rules on students bringing in food and drink from outside after a student took coffee into class on her first day.

Julie Kaputa, an honors student at Beaver River Central School in New York, received an in-school suspension for violating the rule.

#452. How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (934 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.
  • Sources indicate that comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004.
  • On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.

Sources indicate that comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars. Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.

In a recent development, on 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event.

By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August.

Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space.

Industry observers note that models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten.

"We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, noted in a statement.

While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere.

A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes, which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home.

The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter-family comet.

"Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," mentioned Trigo-Rodríguez.

Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune.

Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth.

"Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids.".

Sources indicate that for now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is presently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.

The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

In a recent development, keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

Sony has managed to squeeze out another PlayStation 5 firmware patch before the highly-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto 6.

It has been revealed that sony has been rolling firmware updates out on a fairly regular basis, and like many of those updates, this latest one - version 26.07-14.23.00 - doesn't bring any very meaningful changes. Sony repeated the same "we've made some security fixes to the system software" patch-note that we've seen many times before.

It has been revealed that and like all those firmware updates, 26.07-14.23.00 is mandatory for all PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles, assuming you want to go online or play the latest games. That, of course, includes GTA 6, which requires the console's firmware to be updated to its latest version before you can play.

The update should download automatically the next time you turn on your console, but you can also force the download through Settings > System > System Software > System Software Update and Settings. This is also where you can tick the option for your console to automatically download and install those updates in the future.

Although Sony hasn't directly noted so, the high frequency of those security firmware updates is likely related to the impending release of GTA 6, especially in light of recent gen-AI-driven PS5 jailbreaks.

Sources indicate that any firmware released before GTA 6's release now becomes required to play the game, which delays potential security exploits, seeing as hackers would need to find vulnerabilities in that firmware in order to play. While this may never happen, Sony is at least trying to minimise the risk as much as possible.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

Industry News: AI lets chemists design molecules by simply describing them

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Creating new molecules is one of the toughest tasks in chemistry.
  • In this approach, chemists begin with the final molecule they want and work backward to figure out simpler starting materials and possible reaction routes.
  • Recent findings suggest that another challenge involves reaction mechanisms, which describe how reactions proceed step by step through the movement of electrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Creating new molecules is one of the toughest tasks in chemistry. Whether the goal is a life-saving drug or a cutting-edge material, each compound must be built through a carefully planned series of reactions. Mapping out these steps requires deep expertise and strategic thinking, which is why chemists often spend years mastering the process.

A major hurdle is retrosynthesis. In this approach, chemists begin with the final molecule they want and work backward to figure out simpler starting materials and possible reaction routes. This involves many decisions, such as selecting the right building blocks, deciding when to form rings, and determining whether sensitive parts of the molecule need protection. While computers can scan enormous "chemical spaces," they still struggle to match the strategic judgment of experienced chemists.

Recent findings suggest that another challenge involves reaction mechanisms, which describe how reactions proceed step by step through the movement of electrons. Understanding these mechanisms allows scientists to predict new reactions, improve efficiency, and avoid costly trial and error. Although current computational tools can suggest many possible pathways, they often lack the intuition needed to pinpoint the most realistic ones.

A Newly introduced AI Approach to Chemical Reasoning.

Sources indicate that researchers led by Philippe Schwaller at EPFL have developed a latest method that uses large language models (LLMs) as reasoning tools for chemistry. Rather than directly generating chemical structures, these models act as evaluators that guide existing computational systems.

The fresh framework, called Synthegy, combines traditional search algorithms with AI that can interpret chemical strategies written in natural language.

In a recent development, "When making tools for chemists, the user interface matters a lot, and previous tools relied on cumbersome filters and rules," claims Andres M Bran, the first author of the Synthegy paper published in Matter. "With Synthegy, we're giving chemists the power to just talk, allowing them to iterate much faster and navigate more complex synthetic ideas.".

How Synthegy Improves Retrosynthesis Planning.

Sources indicate that synthegy starts with a target molecule and a simple instruction written in everyday language. For example, a chemist might request that a specific ring be formed early or that unnecessary protecting groups be avoided. Standard retrosynthesis software then generates many possible pathways.

Industry observers note that each of these pathways is converted into text and reviewed by a language model. Synthegy scores how well each option matches the chemist's instructions and explains its reasoning. This makes it easier to rank and filter the best routes. By guiding searches with natural language, chemists can quickly focus on strategies that align with their goals.

Understanding Reaction Mechanisms With AI.

Synthegy applies a similar method to reaction mechanisms. It breaks reactions down into basic electron movements and explores different possibilities. The language model evaluates each step and steers the search toward pathways that make chemical sense.

In a recent development, the system can also incorporate additional details, such as reaction conditions or expert hypotheses, provided as text. This flexibility allows researchers to refine their analysis and explore more realistic scenarios.

Performance and Validation With Chemists.

In a recent development, in synthesis planning, Synthgey was able to identify pathways that matched complex strategic instructions. In a double-blind study, 36 chemists provided 368 valid evaluations, and their assessments agreed with the system's results 71.2% of the time on average.

Recent findings suggest that the framework can flag unnecessary protecting steps, judge how feasible reactions are, and prioritize efficient solutions. It also demonstrates that LLMs can operate at multiple levels, from analyzing functional groups to evaluating entire synthetic routes. Larger models performed best, while smaller ones showed more limited abilities.

According to recent reports, this research highlights a different way AI can support chemistry. Instead of replacing human decision-making, Synthegy positions language models as guides that help interpret and refine computational results. Chemists can describe their goals in plain language and receive solutions that reflect their strategy.

The approach could speed up drug discovery, improve reaction design, and make advanced tools more accessible to scientists.

Industry observers note that "The connection between synthesis planning and mechanisms is very exciting: we usually use mechanisms to discover new reactions that enable us to synthesize new molecules," indicates Andres M Bran. "Our work is bridging that gap computationally through a unified natural language interface.".

Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "fresh" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion.
  • Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant.
  • According to recent reports, "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "fresh" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

According to recent reports, "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the substantial hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

In a recent development, historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

According to recent reports, "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold.".

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

It has been revealed that "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption.".

In a recent development, hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain.".

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very rapidly, in less than a day.".

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. ".

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

According to recent reports, it will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

It has been revealed that want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that when the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage.
  • Industry observers note that three years later, construction began on a new telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

It has been revealed that when the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Industry observers note that three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

Industry observers note that when the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a newly introduced finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus.".

It has been revealed that the collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

In a recent development, "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

A woman splashed out on a $50,000 car so that she could get home during the nationwide air travel stop in the United States, and ended up driving for 27 hours.

Back on November 13, travel plans across the United States were plunged into chaos after a nationwide ground stop was put on planes. The stoppage saw 20,000 flights disrupted, leaving passengers to miss getting home, traveling for work, and delayed for at least a day.

In true Planes, Trains, and Automobiles fashion, some travellers set out to find alternative modes of transport as a result of the group stoppage.

That includes Tara Harding and her employees, as they were trying to get home from Charlotte, North Carolina, to Bismarck, North Dakota.

As per CBS News, Harding, a nurse practitioner, tried to look at alternative flights but ultimately gave up on the idea of flying home.

Instead, her and two colleagues looked at rental cars before deciding to buy a $48,000 Ford Bronco. “If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”.

Harding admitted it is an “insane” idea to splash out on a new car, but the group eventually drove it from the car dealer’s showroom to Bismarck in 27 hours.

The three took turns napping they could drive home without stopping, meaning they’d see their families and not have to reschedule any appointments.

As noted, not everyone was so lucky, with more than 12,000 flights being “unable to recover” and get back on track.

One student pilot was also left in a panic as he was informed of the ground stop while in the air on his first solo cross-country flight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the way people speak during ordinary conversations could offer valuable insight into brain health, according to newly introduced research from Baycrest, the University of Toronto, and York University.
  • According to recent reports, the findings provide some of the strongest evidence so far linking natural speech patterns with key cognitive abilities.
  • "The message is clear: speech timing is more than just a matter of style, it's a sensitive indicator of brain health," says Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the way people speak during ordinary conversations could offer valuable insight into brain health, according to newly introduced research from Baycrest, the University of Toronto, and York University. Scientists found that subtle speech characteristics, including pauses, filler words such as ('uh,' 'um'), and difficulty retrieving words, are closely connected to executive function, the group of mental abilities involved in memory, planning, attention, and flexible thinking.

According to recent reports, the findings provide some of the strongest evidence so far linking natural speech patterns with key cognitive abilities. The work also expands on earlier research showing that older adults who speak more quickly tend to maintain stronger thinking skills over time (Wei et al., 2024).

"The message is clear: speech timing is more than just a matter of style, it's a sensitive indicator of brain health," says Dr. Jed Meltzer, Senior Scientist at Baycrest's Rotman Research Institute and senior author on this study, titled "Natural Speech Analysis Can Reveal Individual Differences in Executive Function Across the Adult Lifespan.".

AI Analysis Reveals Hidden Cognitive Clues.

It has been revealed that for the study, participants were shown detailed images and asked to describe them in their own words. They also completed established tests designed to measure executive function.

In a recent development, researchers then used artificial intelligence to examine the speech recordings in depth. The AI system detected hundreds of subtle speech features, including the length and frequency of pauses, the use of filler words, and timing-related patterns in speech. These markers consistently predicted how well participants performed on cognitive tests, even after researchers adjusted for factors such as age, sex, and education.

Speech Patterns and Dementia Risk.

According to recent reports, executive function naturally weakens with age and is often affected during the early stages of dementia. However, standard cognitive testing can be difficult to repeat frequently because it takes time and people often improve simply from becoming familiar with the tests.

Recent findings suggest that natural speech may offer a simpler alternative. Because speaking is part of daily life, it can be measured repeatedly and unobtrusively on a large scale. Researchers also noted that speech provides valuable insight into processing speed and overall cognitive function in real-world situations, without requiring strict time limits that are common in many traditional cognitive assessments.

The team believes speech analysis could eventually become a practical way to identify people whose cognitive decline is progressing faster than expected and who may face a higher risk of developing dementia.

Recent findings suggest that "This research sets the stage for exciting opportunities to develop tools that could help track cognitive changes in clinics or even at home. Early detection is critical for any cure or intervention, as dementia involves progressive degeneration of the brain that may be slowed," indicates Dr. Meltzer.

Future Research on Brain Health Monitoring.

Sources indicate that the researchers say more long-term studies are needed to follow changes in speech over time and distinguish normal aging from the earliest signs of disease. They also suggest that combining speech analysis with other health measures could make early detection of cognitive decline more accurate, practical, and widely available.

How we test enterprise SSDs

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a hiatus of several years, Tom's Hardware is expanding its in-depth testing and analysis to enterprise and data center SSDs.
  • Recent findings suggest that comprehensive reviews of enterprise and data center SSDs are therefore more key than ever.
  • It has been revealed that reviewing enterprise and data center SSDs required us to build a workstation that could truly challenge these drives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a hiatus of several years, Tom's Hardware is expanding its in-depth testing and analysis to enterprise and data center SSDs. Consumer SSDs and conventional hard drives lack the performance and endurance for extensive AI workloads. This has increased demand for enterprise SSDs. Form factors like U.2, U.3, E3.S, and E1.S, once rare, are now common in high-end workstations and home labs. These enterprise storage solutions provide higher capacities, better performance, and greater reliability than consumer drives.

Recent findings suggest that comprehensive reviews of enterprise and data center SSDs are therefore more key than ever. Buying a drive of this caliber is a major decision and a significant investment for organizations of all sizes. With this latest venture, Tom's Hardware will continue to help buyers make informed decisions with comprehensive reviews and performance analyses.

It has been revealed that reviewing enterprise and data center SSDs required us to build a workstation that could truly challenge these drives. This project would not have been possible without the support of several component makers, including Asus, Corsair, G.Skill, Icy Dock, and Noctua, who made the workstation a reality, a challenging prospect in the current market.

Recent findings suggest that the Xeon 658X, a 24-core, 48-thread chip from the Granite Rapids family with a 4.9 GHz boost clock speed, powers the testing workstation. Single-core performance and total core count matter just as much when reviewing storage. Clock speed determines how many IOPS one core can push and how fast it answers a single request, while 24 cores let us spread a drive's load across eight fio jobs and later test several drives at once. The Xeon 658X ticks all those boxes.

According to recent reports, we've entrusted the Xeon 658X's cooling to Noctua's NH-U14S DX-4677 air cooler, which supports both LGA4677 and LGA4710 sockets. The single-tower CPU air cooler delivers high-performance cooling at very low noise levels thanks to its dual NF-A15 140mm cooling fans.

In a recent development, with its server-grade components and robust enterprise features, the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE is the ideal motherboard to pair with the Xeon 658X. Its extensive feature set includes an onboard MCIO x8 connection, split into x4/x4, that allows for evaluating two U.2 or U.3 drives. The board also provides seven PCIe 5.0 expansion slots (six at x16 and one at x8) to fully leverage the Xeon 658X’s 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes, so the SSDs and graphics cards never hit bandwidth limits.

We're still in need of support for an RTX Pro graphics card, which would be an invaluable asset for enterprise SSD reviews for real-world AI workloads, but our current test platform allows us to test the most important aspects of performance.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite the memory and storage shortage, G.Skill and Corsair have stepped up to provide crucial components for our enterprise SSD test bench. G.Skill sent a G5 DDR5-6400 C32 64GB (4x16GB) R-DIMM memory kit, which runs at the stock DDR5-5600 speed. The decision to keep it at the JEDEC baseline has nothing to do with the memory kit: Memory frequency does not affect performance in enterprise SSD tests.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Corsair provided the speedy MP700 Pro XT 2TB, one of the best SSDs, as the test bench's primary storage. The PCIe 5.0 drive delivers sequential read and write speeds up to 14,900 MB/s and 14,500 MB/s, respectively, and keeps the workstation snappy, especially when it hammers enterprise drives all day long.

Industry observers note that no power supply is better suited to the job than the Corsair HX1500i. It offers a massive 1,500W capacity with plenty of headroom for future upgrades, and it runs quietly and stably, two qualities that matter when you keep the test system running for countless hours. It is an 80 Plus Platinum power supply with at least 89% efficiency at full load.

Testing enterprise drives in a standard PCIe expansion slot is more convenient. For that purpose, Icy Dock has provided us with the ExpressSlot Elite MB221E5P-B and MB303E5P-B to accept one and two E1.S SSDs. Unlike other generic designs on the market, these adapters feature tool-less installation mechanisms that don't require removing them from the PCIe expansion slot, and they include 50mm fans for active cooling.

The list also included the ToughArmor MB218E5P-B, a 5.25-inch drive bay that supports up to eight E1.S SSDs for future projects exploring RAID arrays. To test E3.S drives, we use a JMT ADT-R27C adapter strapped to a Noctua NF-F12 industrialPPC-24V-3000 IP67 PWM cooling fan, which can run at 12V and still provide substantial airflow to actively cool the SSDs under evaluation.

Sources indicate that A TGDGamer E-ATX test bench houses the hardware for the enterprise SSD system. It may not look flashy, but it does the job, and that is what matters. As an open-air test bench, it is easy to install and remove hardware, and it eliminates variables when it comes to heat generation and buildup. The test bench also supports motherboard form factors up to SSI-EEB, so the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE feels right at home.

In a recent development, A spec sheet only tells you what a drive can do on its best day. The real world is not as pretty. The drive is mostly full, garbage collection is constantly at work, and multiple workloads are hitting it simultaneously. Our enterprise benchmark suite is built to measure the drive in service: at steady state, under load, through write bursts, and with other jobs running. Every drive gets the same automated run on the same test bench. Every result is stored with the exact parameters that produced it, so we can trace how we got there.

Sources indicate that this can take some time. A full run takes most of a day on a 7.68TB PCIe 5.0 drive, and it writes the drive end-to-end many times over. To make life a bit easier on us, the benchmark can be run unattended, and it’s crash-resumable from the last stage. A shorter express mode handles bench checks and quick triage. When a result looks odd, express runs and variant runs, which repeat just the tests in question or change one setting, help us find the cause before we take it to the vendor.

We run the bench on a custom Debian 13 image that we build and maintain ourselves, with the suite copied in at build time. This image gets installed on the bench’s OS drive, and the kernel is pinned so every drive has the same software stack. Right now that’s Linux 7.2.6 from Debian backports, because Debian 13’s stock 6.12 kernel predates support for the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE’s Intel E610 10GbE controller. The suite is also designed to be run remotely if needed, but we need a tester at the bench to switch the drives, of course.

Industry observers note that debian is our pick over Ubuntu for a few reasons: it has fewer background services, no Snap, and no unattended upgrades by default. We hold the kernel so nothing changes between runs. We remove AppArmor and turn off scheduled jobs that could fire mid-run, like the weekly TRIM timer and the drive-health service that polls every drive, and the suite records any that are still running. The suite also turns off NVMe autonomous power-state transitions (APST) at the start of every run and checks that the drive reports it off, so no drive drops into a low-power state during an idle gap and adds wake-up latency to the next I/O.

Sources indicate that every test runs in fio 3.42, using io_uring and direct I/O against the raw block device. This means no filesystem and no page cache sitting between fio and the drive; the bench’s 64GB of RAM never caches a byte of test data. We compile fio from source because Debian’s packaged version lacks SPRandom, which we’ll get to in short order.

It has been revealed that some enterprise storage reviews run application profiles in Oracle’s Vdbench, but we decided to go full fio. This makes for a more consistent suite with one set of latency accounting across every chart. And fio is open source and actively maintained, while Vdbench hasn’t had a new release since 2018. Vdbench profiles are built from the same parts fio uses, such as read/write ratio, block-size mix, and random or sequential access, and our mixed-workload sweeps cover the common read/write ratios at 4K and 8K, though not mixed-block-size profiles. Running Vdbench ourselves wouldn’t make our results comparable to other outlets’ anyway, since they use different hardware, preconditioning, and profile definitions.

According to recent reports, A key element of benchmarking SSDs is making sure the test drive is at steady state, with the performance it can sustain rather than the peak you can see after a fresh erase. Our first stage is a secure erase using nvme format. If a drive refuses, the suite falls back to a plain format, then a full-drive discard, and records which one it used.

In a recent development, next comes preconditioning. SPRandom, SanDisk’s open-source contribution to fio, is a faster alternative to filling the drive over and over for hours. It takes user capacity and over-provisioning (OP) as inputs, which SanDisk notes lets it reach a steady-state layout in just one pass. Overprovisioning (OP) is inferred from the capacity point or given by the tester. NVMe drives don’t report their raw flash, so a 7.68TB drive like our first one, assumed to sit on 8TiB of actual NAND, works out to having about 14.5% OP.

We don’t take SPRandom’s result on faith. A steady-state gate follows, running 4K random writes at queue depth 256 (QD256) until the drive’s write speed stops moving. It uses the two tests from the Storage Networking Industry Association’s (SNIA) steady-state rule, with limits ten times tighter, applied to the last 30 minutes: split into five six-minute rounds, the round averages must sit within 2% of one another, and the trend line across the window can’t move more than 1%.

Sources indicate that that takes a while, but that’s the point: an earlier, looser version of the gate passed our first drive while its write speed was still climbing. The whole settling curve is saved with every run, and a drive that doesn’t settle within three hours is marked as not reaching steady state, though the run continues. As a backstop, the suite repeats the four-corner 4K write after the random sweep, hours later, and flags the run if the two results differ by more than 3%.

Recent findings suggest that the suite also checks its own results as it goes. If a test’s slowest moment falls below 70% of its average, that test is run again on the spot. If a point in the random sweep lands more than 10% off the curve set by its neighbors, it’s measured again before the drive is erased for the sequential tests. Both results are kept, and any re-test is noted in the review.

Following the random tests, the tool erases the drive again and writes it end to end once, with 128K sequential writes at QD64. We run it before the sequential and AI tests, so the drive is conditioned with the kind of I/O we’re about to measure. It matters because sequential writes can swing wildly on a randomly written drive: on our first test drive, the fastest result was more than three times the slowest. After a sequential fill, they held flat from QD2 through QD1024, at both 128K and 1MB.

Sources indicate that drives are formatted to 512-byte logical blocks when they support it, so our block size sweep can go down to 512-byte transfers, which a 4K-native namespace can’t issue. SNIA’s enterprise IOPS test uses 512-byte transfers too, and Kioxia pitches 512-byte access for its GP Series, which is aimed at GPU-initiated storage. Drives without a 512-byte format are tested as shipped, and their sub-4K results are marked unsupported. The switch happens in the same format command as the secure erase, so it adds no time.

According to recent reports, A fast enough SSD will happily benchmark your host, or your tools, instead, and our early runs turned up three ways that could happen. The first is CPU idle states, or C-states: waking our Xeon 658X cores from their deepest idle state can take up to 170 microseconds, and at QD1 that directly impacts the results. Holding the cores awake for the whole run cut the first drive’s average 4K QD1 read latency by about a sixth.

The second is the CPU itself: a single fio job can saturate its core well short of what a PCIe 5.0 drive can manage. Split across eight jobs, the same test runs several times faster, so random tests now spread their queue depth across up to eight fio jobs. That’s also why fast cores, and enough of them, matter for this test bench.

The third is fio itself. By default, fio seeds its random generator the same way every run, so it replays the same sequence of random offsets, and each random write test rewrites the previous test’s blocks in the same order. On our first drive, that was the main reason 4K random writes came in at more than twice the sustained figure. Every random test now runs with a fresh random seed.

It has been revealed that what we don’t change matters, too. Completions arrive by interrupt rather than polling, and the IOMMU stays in its default mode, because that’s how most applications use a drive. On our first drive, polling and IOMMU passthrough would each have shaved some latency off 4K QD1 writes.

According to recent reports, interrupts also set a ceiling at the other end of the scale: this bench tops out near 2.8 million 4K random read IOPS, and adding fio jobs doesn’t lift it, though polling does. So on the fastest drives, our 4K random read result can sit below the spec sheet’s, and that’s our bench’s limit, not the drive’s. Our low queue depth latencies, writes especially, run higher than a tuned host would show, but they’re closer to what you’d actually see. To show the drive’s limit at both ends, the suite repeats three tests with polled I/O at the end of the random stage: the 4K random read peak, plus 4K random reads and writes at QD1. Those results get their own charts and never mix into the main ones.

4K random read and write at QD256; 128K and 1MB sequential read and write at QD64.

The headline numbers, measured on a preconditioned drive instead of fresh out of the box.

4K and 8K, QD1 to QD4096, eight read/write mixes from 100% read to 100% write.

Servers rarely run flat out; QD1 is what latency-bound software feels, and 8K is a common database page size.

4K random read at QD1024 across eight jobs, plus 4K random read and write at QD1, all with polled I/O.

What the drive can do with the host’s interrupt overhead out of the way; the results to set against a spec sheet.

128K and 1MB sequential reads and writes, QD1 to QD1024.

How much parallelism a drive needs to reach full speed; low queue depths are what a single restore or scan gets.

Random reads and writes from 512 bytes to 1MB at QD32.

Writes smaller than a drive’s mapping unit can pay a read-modify-write penalty; large blocks show its bandwidth cap.

4K and 8K reads and writes at QD1, QD4, and QD16, from the median (P50) to the 99.999th percentile (P99.999).

Averages hide the stalls applications notice; at a million IOPS, the slowest 0.001% is still ten requests a second.

4K 70/30 at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, plotted as a share of the drive’s own peak.

Finds the load where latency starts to climb.

One hour of 4K random writes at QD256.

Whether sustained writes hold a flat line or sawtooth as garbage collection struggles.

4K QD1 reads for four minutes right after a heavy write burst.

How far reads drop after heavy writes, and how fast they recover.

Write bursts after idle gaps of 0 to 300 seconds.

How much write speed a quiet spell buys back.

Database I/O patterns (simulated).

4K QD1 log writes with a sync after each, a random 8K 70/30 mix at QD16, and a 256K sequential read scan.

Log-write latency, page I/O, and analytics scans, without benchmarking a database’s RAM cache.

Checkpoint-sized saves and restores modeled on 8B- and 70B-class models (105GiB over eight writers, 912GiB over 64).

Time until the slowest writer finishes, which is when a real checkpoint would be done.

A fixed 4K read load, alone and during a checkpoint save.

What a checkpoint does to serving traffic on the same drive.

Drive temperature through the hour-long sustained write test.

Measured against the drive’s own warning and critical thresholds.

Some things are out of scope by design. We review drives; we don’t certify them. That rules out dual-port failover, power-loss validation, and single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV), which belong in a qualification lab. We’ll add tests when they prove themselves on the bench. Many of the tests in the table are old standbys and still earn their place. Others are newer and require further explanation.

In a recent development, for one, we chart latency against load: the 70/30 4K mix from the random sweep, at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, with throughput shown as a share of the drive’s own peak. Tail latency climbs as the load grows, and the point where it turns sharply upward (on our first drive, that was write latency) represents the practical operating ceiling, or the load you can strategy a server around without giving up low latency.

Sources indicate that we also test write-to-read recovery, which measures how a drive’s reads hold up after a heavy write burst. A few minutes of 4K random writes at QD256 leave the drive with cleanup to do, and QD1 reads are then timed over the next four minutes. If a drive is still busy collecting garbage, it will read slower before climbing back; the extent and duration of the drop are the result.

Idle recovery measures what downtime buys back. After a minute of sustained writes, the drive sits idle for anywhere from zero to five minutes, then a 10-second write burst, logged second by second, indicates whether background cleanup freed enough blocks to run faster.

It has been revealed that checkpoint interference indicates what an AI checkpoint does to anything else sharing the drive. A light 4K read load, which stands in for inference or database queries, runs alone, and then again during a checkpoint save. Each read is timed from when it was due, not when it was sent, so reads stuck waiting behind a stalled one count too.

Sources indicate that lastly, we test thermals. Drive temperature is tracked through the hour-long sustained write test and charted against the drive's own warning and critical thresholds.

The full process means every drive is treated the same and compared fairly, with a method built to give the same results run after run. This allows us to provide a level playing field built on accurate and repeatable performance characterization.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

"Encouraging players to return is no mean feat" - Square Enix tempts Final Fantasy 14 players back with free game-time to fill void before upcoming expansion

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that final Fantasy 14 is between expansions at the moment, with Evercold preparing for release in February.
  • Industry observers note that this promotion, which began yesterday, offers players a choice between two enticing freebies.
  • Recent findings suggest that in addition, there's an alluring character skip available too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that final Fantasy 14 is between expansions at the moment, with Evercold preparing for release in February. So, in order to keep the game populated for the next few months, Square Enix is running a special promotion in hopes of tempting players back in.

Industry observers note that this promotion, which began yesterday, offers players a choice between two enticing freebies. Lapsed players who haven't logged in for over six months are to be given 30 days of free game time to hop back in and catch up with the main story quest ahead of Evercold's release.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, there's an alluring character skip available too. If your FF14 character is at least level 90 on one class - the current level-cap is 100 - you can skip all the way to the final part of the latest Dawntrail expansion. You still need to grind to level 100 in preparation for Evercold, but the aforementioned free month of game time should provide plenty of time to do so.

In a producer letter written to accompany this promotion, Naoki Yoshida provided insight into why this was being implemented, stating that retaining players in an MMO like FF14 was of the "utmost importance".

It has been revealed that "Encouraging players to return is no mean feat", Yoshida wrote. "People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons, including dissatisfaction and loss of interest. Although we continually update the game to address such complications, the fact remains that getting players to resume their journey is a difficult task indeed.

"For one, I feel that the pace of change in our lives is growing increasingly fast. Back when A Realm Reborn launched, I set policies in place based on the idea that significant changes in life usually happened in roughly three-year cycles. With that in mind, we've done our best to avoid heavy-handed attempts to secure player retention through game design, and we still maintain that philosophy even today.".

Yoshida went on to explain that promotions such as this are meant as a "tiny nudge". He notes that those who have retained subscriptions continuously remain "the most notable" players in the development team's eyes, and acknowledges that the process of catching up in an MMO can seem "daunting" for many.

This problem of player retention is nothing newly introduced for MMOs, especially in the tricky time between the end of a current expansion and the beginning of a new one. MMO popularity often waxes and wanes, with a new expansion acting as an exciting call to action, with the months leading up to it often serving as a natural break-point for many. Still, monthly subs pay the bills, so keeping folks around even during these quiet months is important.

Final Fantasy 14: Evercold is looking like an especially exciting expansion. On top of the new story and two classes being added, the game is getting an overhaul to combat, with both classic Reborn and Evolved action modes, as well as a new raid difficulty meant to bridge the gap between normal and savage tiers.

The game has certainly come a long way since its initial release back in 2010. Dawntrail proved divisive among fans too, though with Evercold there's a lot of hope that a upcoming overarching storyline can bring the steal back the hearts of players old and new.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A São Paulo businessman has been arrested by police on suspicion of sending a game console stuffed with explosives to the electronics store of a rival in an attempt to kill him. The device then exploded. On Monday, Military Police executed a warrant against Everton Yoshizumi Lima, who is suspected of perpetrating the outrageous attack, G1 reports.

On October 23, 2026, at around 5:30 pm, a delivery person dropped off a video game console at an electronics repair shop, with the cover that it was being left for modifications requested by the customer. Police say the device had an explosive planted inside that was programmed to detonate upon receipt. "Unaware of its contents, the store owner put the video game console in a drawer and continued working," the report states. The device ignited and exploded, causing severe damage and injuring two people: the owner of the store and a friend who was at the scene. The whole thing was captured on video, which you can see by expanding the tweet below:.

Empresário é preso suspeito de enviar videogame com explosivos que detonaram em loja de eletrônicos de Santo André, Grande SP https://t.co/EqXSlkM1J9 #g1 https://t.co/H3naAgNzlVNovember 16, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the device was found to have two explosive charges of the same magnitude inside, but only one of the devices went off, possibly limiting the capacity for damage and injury. The report notes that investigators believe the intent of the device was to kill the victim, given the amount of explosives. The console was delivered to the store by an unsuspecting motorcyclist who was working for a delivery app company and had no idea they were carrying a bomb.

Sources indicate that the request appears to have been traced back to Lima, who is the main suspect in the attack. Lima purportedly owns other electronics stores in the area, including two on the same street where this store was recently opened, labeling the motive as "business competition." "The new store had been advertised through a social media campaign and the distribution of flyers," the report states. "Annoyed by the competition, the suspect allegedly decided to eliminate the competitor, according to the line of investigation.".

According to the report, Lima was arrested during the course of an investigation into a possible motorcycle theft. It appears that Lima was the owner of the target vehicle, and that police visited in advance, suspecting someone might try to steal it. While checking his data, it was found that Lima had an outstanding arrest warrant for his suspected involvement in the attack.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions.
  • Researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials.
  • Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions. In some cases, scientists can even create entirely newly introduced quantum properties by carefully changing a material's structure. One striking example involves stacking sheets of graphene and twisting them into a moiré pattern, which can suddenly turn the material into a superconductor.

Researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials. But predicting how these exotic materials will behave is extraordinarily difficult. Quasicrystals are so mathematically complex that simulating them can involve more than a quadrillion numbers, a scale far beyond the reach of today's most powerful supercomputers.

Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem.

Scientists at Aalto University's Department of Applied Physics have now developed a quantum-inspired algorithm capable of handling these enormous non-periodic quantum materials almost instantly. Assistant Professor Jose Lado indicates the work also highlights a promising feedback cycle within quantum technology itself.

"Crucially, these new quantum algorithms can enable the development of new quantum materials to build new paradigms of quantum computers, creating a productive two-way feedback loop between quantum materials and quantum computers," he explains.

The advance could eventually support the development of dissipationless electronics, which conduct electricity without energy loss. Such systems may help reduce the growing heat and energy demands of AI-driven data centers.

In a recent development, the research team was led by Lado and included doctoral researcher Tiago Antão, who served as the paper's main author; QDOC doctoral researcher Yitao Sun; and Academy Research Fellow Adolfo Fumega. Their findings were recently published in Physical Review Letters as an Editor's Suggestion.

Simulating Topological Quasicrystals.

The researchers focused on topological quasicrystals, unusual materials that host unconventional quantum excitations. These excitations are especially valuable because they help protect electrical conductivity from disruptive noise and interference. However, they are distributed unevenly throughout the already highly complex structure of a quasicrystal.

Rather than attempting to directly calculate the full structure of the material, the team reformulated the challenge using methods similar to those used by quantum computers.

"Quantum computers work in exponentially large computational spaces, so we used a special family of algorithms to encode those spaces, known as tensor networks, to compute a quasicrystal with over 268 million sites. Our algorithm shows how colossal problems in quantum materials can be directly solved with the exponential speed-up that comes from encoding the problem as a quantum many-body system," Antão notes.

At this stage, the work remains theoretical and was carried out through simulations, but researchers say experimental testing and future applications are already coming into view.

"The quantum-inspired algorithm we demonstrated enables us to create super-moiré quasicrystals several orders of magnitude above the capabilities of conventional methods. That is an instrumental step towards designing topological qubits with super-moiré materials for use in quantum computers, for example," Lado says.

Toward Practical Quantum Computing Applications.

According to Lado, the algorithm could eventually be adapted to operate on actual quantum computers once the hardware becomes sufficiently advanced.

"Our method can be adapted to run on real quantum computers, once they reach necessary scale and fidelity. In particular, the new AaltoQ20 and the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure can play a significant role for future demonstrations," Lado notes.

The findings suggest that studying and designing exotic quantum materials may become one of the earliest practical applications for quantum algorithms and quantum computing systems.

The project also brings together two major areas of Finnish quantum research: quantum materials and quantum algorithms. It is part of Lado's ERC Consolidator grant ULTRATWISTROICS, which focuses on designing topological qubits using van der Waals materials, as well as the Center of Excellence in Quantum Materials QMAT, whose goal is to advance the quantum technologies of the future.

30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
