📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the very popular and critically-acclaimed The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has set another record. After selling 5.2m copies in four days and becoming the Switch 2's fastest-selling game, Ocarina of Time has now been revealed to also be a major seller at retail.

The remake has sold more than 1m physical copies in the US alone in its launch week (ending 7th November). That's according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, who revealed on Bluesky that the record also makes it the first title to surpass 1m physical sales since 2023's Tears of the Kingdom. That is, no other game - from any publisher - has managed to sell over 1m copies in the US within its first week in three years.

According to recent reports, while Nintendo games tend to perform better at retail than those from Sony, Xbox or third-party publishers, physical sales in general have been declining in the US. In July, Piscatella revealed that just seven PlayStation games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies up to that point in 2026, and that was after all the backlash to Sony's decision to end physical disc manufacturing by January 2028.

Ocarina of Time's lead of this particular segment likely won't continue, however. That's because, as Piscatella pointed out in a follow-up post, Circana's tracking considers disc-less, code-in-box versions to be physical editions. This means Grand Theft Auto 6 will likely overtake the remake in short order, just as it's expected to break records elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's glowing review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Christian Donlan argued that Nintendo has done just enough to modernise a timeless classic while maintaining what made the original so special for many players.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

It has been revealed that "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

In a recent development, the FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.).

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Recent findings suggest that dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

It has been revealed that dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

In a recent development, the manufacturer is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

#419. A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

📅 10 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (759 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

📅 10 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task.
  • The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems. But new research suggests they may struggle with something humans do every day: staying focused on the task at hand when distractions get in the way.

Recent findings suggest that researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task. The results revealed a significant difference between how AI systems process information and how the human brain manages attention.

The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.

In the test, color words such as "red," "blue," or "green" are displayed in colored ink. Sometimes the word and the ink color match. For example, the word "red" might appear in red ink. Other times they conflict, such as the word "red" printed in blue ink.

Participants are asked to name the color of the ink rather than read the word itself.

That sounds simple, but it creates a challenge because reading words is an automatic habit for most people. The brain must suppress the urge to read the word and instead focus on identifying the ink color.

Psychologists often use the task to measure what is known as executive control, a set of mental processes that helps people regulate attention, resist distractions, and stay focused on goals.

The researchers wanted to see whether modern large language models (LLMs) handle this challenge in the same way humans do.

According to recent reports, LLMs are the AI systems behind tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. They are trained on enormous amounts of text and learn patterns in language, allowing them to generate responses that often appear remarkably human.

When given short lists containing five color words, the AI systems generally performed well, even when the words and colors did not match.

However, the picture changed dramatically as the lists became longer.

According to recent reports, GPT-4o achieved 91% accuracy when working with five words. At ten words, its accuracy fell to 57%. When the list expanded to forty words, accuracy dropped to just 15%.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintained stable performance through lists of twenty words but then experienced a sharp decline, falling to 24% accuracy with forty-word lists.

The researchers observed similar patterns in GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and Gemini 2.5.

The challenge became even more difficult when matching and mismatched color words appeared together in the same list.

Under those conditions, performance deteriorated further. Accuracy for the mismatched items dropped to nearly zero in some cases.

Industry observers note that according to the researchers, the AI models had trouble maintaining the instruction to identify ink colors. Instead, they increasingly defaulted to reading the words themselves.

In other words, the systems appeared unable to consistently suppress the response they had been most heavily trained to produce.

This finding is particularly interesting because humans face a similar conflict. People are generally much better at reading words than naming ink colors. Yet despite this bias, most individuals can maintain high accuracy and stable performance even when confronted with long lists of conflicting words and colors.

Human Attention vs. Machine Attention.

The study highlights an important distinction between human and artificial intelligence.

Although modern AI systems can produce impressive language and reasoning capabilities, their underlying mechanisms differ from the attention processes found in biological brains.

Humans can often sustain focus on a specific goal while filtering out competing information. The results suggest that current AI models may struggle with this type of cognitive control when tasks become increasingly demanding.

In a recent development, the researchers argue that the performance collapse seen in these experiments points to fundamental limitations in today's large language models. While AI can sometimes mimic human behavior, its ability to maintain attention appears to operate very differently from the way people do.

The findings offer a reminder that even the most advanced AI systems still have weaknesses, particularly when tasks require them to resist distractions and stay focused over extended sequences of information.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products.
  • Sources indicate that over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference.
  • To make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products. FP64, or double-precision floating-point math, is widely used in the high-performance scientific computing and simulation fields that are the focus of SC26. For those customers, AMD is trumpeting the value of its latest Instinct MI430X accelerator for customers that still need native FP64, like national laboratories and supercomputing centers.

Sources indicate that over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference. That reallocation only makes business sense, as the total addressable market for AI compute has exploded while the demand for double-precision math in large supercomputing installations has remained flat by comparison.

To make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes. But AMD claims this kind of emulation is nowhere close to a replacement for native double-precision processing for a few reasons—hence continued development of specialized products like the MI430X.

It has been revealed that for one, AMD notes that Ozaki emulation assumes that the workload in question resembles a dense general matrix multiply (GEMM). In its own application profiling, the company says "less than 10%" of HPC workloads perform dense GEMM operations, so this emulation is a good replacement for native compute. Dense linear algebra is the one common workload for which AMD says Ozaki emulation is a natural fit.

For workloads like sparse iterative linear algebra, stencils and hydrodynamics, high-order finite element analysis, Monte Carlo and particle transport, and classical molecular dynamics, AMD indicates developers still need strong FP64 vector performance for the best results.

Furthermore, even for workloads that map well onto GEMM operations, AMD says matrix sizes must be large in order to achieve the best performance, and that might also not be a given for every operation. The operands of those matrices also have to be sized well to the hardware, as incorrectly scaled operands can reduce performance. The FP64 vector math capabilities of the MI430X are insensitive to those operand sizing complications.

Beyond those stumbling blocks, AMD also notes that using Ozaki emulation methods can cause the memory footprint of an application to balloon, requiring up to three times more capacity than native FP64 would.

Since HBM capacity is directly tied to GPUs in modern supercomputing installations, fitting a workload to a machine that can only emulate FP64 operations could have cascading effects on the number of GPUs and compute nodes required, causing knock-on challenges for the floor area, power, and cooling required to support the system.

AMD indicates the high 432GB of HBM4 memory capacity per MI430X node allows its customers to provision fewer GPUs and compute nodes in a system, saving on networking, power, and floor space.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to its FP64 HPC performance, AMD positions an MI430X-powered supercomputer as an AI inference platform for developing workloads that utilize those models as part of the research process. But there are some key differences between those systems and the Helios rack-scale accelerator powered by MI455X GPUs from the same CDNA 5 architectural family.

Each MI430X GPU offers 9.2 PFLOPS of theoretical FP4 compute performance for inference, but that should be understood in the context of the whopping 40.3 PFLOPS of FP4 compute from each AI-focused MI455X accelerator.

Beyond raw performance, the native scale-up domain size of four MI430Xs over AMD’s Infinity Fabric interconnect when coupled with a sixth-generation EPYC host CPU pales in comparison to the domain size of 72 MI455X accelerators in a Helios rack. AMD notes this interconnect is optimized more for latency-sensitive operations rather than a massive scale-up domain.

Of course, every customer and user of such a system will have different requirements, and institutional supercomputing installations usually aren’t trying to do double duty as cloud inference providers.

For scientists and engineers whose AI models of choice work well within the 1.72 TB of aggregate HBM4 capacity and 93.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth offered by four MI430X's working together across the 12.3 Tbps of scale-up bandwidth available within such a node, the inference performance of each node is likely more than up to the task of the kinds of AI applications that need to be run alongside double-precision compute workloads.

In a recent development, in any event, the MI430X can already count several supercomputing design wins in its corner. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Alice Recoque installation in France, the LUMI-AI system at Finland’s CSC, and the Herder system in Germany will all take advantage of the native FP64 support offered by the MI430X.

AMD’s continued support for native FP64, even as Nvidia retreats from that capability in its products, will doubtless be a point of pride for its architects and engineers, even as those institutional supercomputers will be dwarfed by both AMD and Nvidia-powered AI inference installations the world over. The firm's semi-custom silicon design chops and chiplet experience give it the flexibility needed to tailor products like the MI430X to these specialized markets instead of pursuing a one-size-fits-all approach.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sci-fi role-playing game Exodus continues to play into the Mass Effect comparisons by revealing the female version of its main character Jun, and with studio Archetype referring to her in marketing material as FemJun.

In a recent development, if that moniker sounds familiar it's because it is: the female Commander Shepard character in the Mass Effect series was nicknamed FemShep. FemShep became an iconic part of BioWare's iconic series, eventually proving that female leads could front games just as successfully as male leads could, and be every bit as popular.

It has been revealed that is the nickname FemJun too blatant? Possibly. But there's well publicised BioWare pedigree at Archetype Entertainment, in the studio's co-founders and in the people leading the project. Key Mass Effect writer Drew Karpyshyn is in charge of writing Exodus, for example, and the similarities to Mass Effect are something the Exodus team has not been shy about in the past. In the wake of Mass Effect 5 being cancelled and BioWare being closed, they become even more alluring.

There are, however, big and key differences between Exodus and Mass Effect, key among them, time dilation. In Exodus, there are special Exodus missions whereby you leave your home planet and fly far away, and in doing so experience time differently to the people back home. Many years will pass for them while only days will pass for you, which provides the game with a way to show you long-term consequences of your actions when you return.

In a recent development, archetype hasn't shown the female version of Jun before, despite having released many videos of Exodus, perhaps to build anticipation for her reveal. It's a press beat that's also provided Archetype - a studio owned by Dungeons & Dragons manufacturer Wizards of the Coast - with an occasion to reveal the two actors playing Jun in the game.

Recent findings suggest that female Jun is portrayed by Carina Conti, who played the lead in the recent Mafia game, The Old Country - Isabella Torrisi. She's appeared in HBO's Winning Time and Hulu/Freeform's Good Trouble as well. Male Jun, meanwhile, is portrayed by Stephen Oyoung, who played Mister Negative in Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 1 and 2 games, and Red Hood in Gotham Knights. He also appeared in Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, The Wrecking Crew, and Twisters. The game also famously stars Matthew McConaughey.

Recent findings suggest that archetype announced a Dark Horse hardback art book to go on sale alongside the game next year as well. This arrives a week after the game; Exodus arrives 7th April 2027 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X, and the art book on 13th April.

Industry observers note that matt played Exodus at Gamescom relatively recently and came away impressed, referring to it as "the best kind of surprise". "I wasn't expecting quite such a bombastic 45 minutes when I first picked up a controller and settled into Exodus, admittedly, but the more I played, the more it made sense," he wrote. "I might not be much of a Mass Effect fan (damn you M35 Mako once more), but Exodus is now firmly on my radar ahead of its arrival next year.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

In a recent development, the Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

Recent findings suggest that "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, stated in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something latest to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

It has been revealed that this finding demonstrates that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

In a recent development, chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness).
  • In a recent development, the case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness). The judgment came after a 30-day Competition Appeal Tribunal that took place in London, where PlayStation users claimed Sony had removed "all actual and potential competition" in relation to selling digital games on the console.

In a recent development, the case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store. In a judgment published by the London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today (17th November), the case was rejected. The judgement noted that market definitions used to define Sony's conduct were "unsafe", and that consumers "would be likely to make informed choices when purchasing consoles" and games on the hardware, too.

"Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value people who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.

It has been revealed that the lawsuit made the argument that, upon purchasing a PS5 or other PlayStation console, you were then trapped within its ecosystem, and forced into paying the prices determined by Sony. The Tribunal disagreed, however, and ruled that Sony competed within a wider 'systems market' alongside Xbox, Nintendo and PC, for example. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no evidence that the existence of other digital storefronts would have actually brought any PlayStation Store pricing down.

According to recent reports, interestingly, the Tribunal used the argument that consumers can also opt and buy physical games instead of using the PlayStation Store - something that is changing as of the start of 2028. That did not seem to have any bearing on today's decision, though. It's also worth noting that this case did not seek to interrogate the ownership status of digital games - something that's been at the heart of the movement rallying against Sony's decision to kill off physical media. Earlier this year, spokespeople from Sony's legal team argued "reasonable consumers" already know they don't actually own their digital games.

In a recent development, the London Tribunal has a fairly long history. Back in 2022, it began as a case that attempted to sue Sony to the tune of £5bn for "ripping people off" on PlayStation Store. Sony argued the case brought against it in this trial was "flawed from start to finish". This isn't the only situation where we're seeing consumers pursue legal action against the platform holder. Last year, PlayStation was sued in the Netherlands over the so-called "Sony tax" that highlighted artificially inflated prices on the Store, and sought to represent more than 20,000 participants that felt short-changed by the manufacturer.

Latest Update: Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions.
  • The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang.
  • Recent findings suggest that quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions. The team, from HKU's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Centre for Advanced Semiconductors and Integrated Circuits (CASIC), developed a programmable neuromorphic hardware platform capable of operating at temperatures near absolute zero.

The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang. Their work introduces a new method for generating and controlling negative differential resistance (NDR) in industry standard Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs. Using this approach, the researchers demonstrated for the first time that a single transistor can reproduce the energy efficient "spiking" activity of biological neurons at temperatures as low as 10mK.

Brain-Inspired Hardware for Quantum Computing.

Recent findings suggest that quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures. Existing silicon based control systems consume considerable power and produce unwanted heat, making it necessary to position them away from the qubits themselves. That distance creates extensive wiring requirements that can hinder performance and make large scale quantum computers more difficult to build.

"Our work introduces a hardware platform that can be integrated alongside quantum processors," said Professor Zhang. "By using the unique carrier dynamics in silicon carbide, we can create circuits that are thousands of times more energy-efficient than conventional electronics, significantly reducing the thermal load on cryogenic systems.".

Silicon Carbide Reveals Unique Cryogenic Behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the team found that SiC MOSFETs display a strong "S-shape" NDR effect when cooled below 2K. This behavior is driven by electron-donor impact ionization (EDII). Unlike other technologies that depend on heat generated within a device, the newly observed mechanism arises directly from the material's atomic properties. As a result, it remains highly stable and can be reproduced consistently across different manufacturing batches.

It has been revealed that "This is a robust and scalable approach," said Mr. Yang. "Because SiC is already used globally in electric vehicles and power grids, we can leverage existing industrial foundries to manufacture these cryogenic chips on 300-mm wafers.".

From Artificial Neurons to Deep Space Missions.

Industry observers note that the study also demonstrated that these artificial neurons can be linked together, or "cascaded," into larger networks. This capability could enable advanced local data processing at cryogenic temperatures and improve key quantum computing functions such as quantum error correction and real time quantum control.

The potential applications extend well beyond quantum computing. Because the circuits are designed to operate reliably in extremely cold environments, they could also be valuable for deep space exploration. Future systems may be able to function in the harsh conditions found on the Moon's surface or in the distant regions of our solar system.

The findings were published in Nature Communications in a paper titled "Cryogenic neuromorphic circuits using gate-controlled negative differential resistance in silicon carbide.".

For now, Nvidia's former CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. Kress hasn't had long to settle in ahead of the first massive test — the company's first earnings call since the scandal will take place today, November 17.

#411. Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years

Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.
  • In a recent development, despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.
  • Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

In a recent development, despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you.".

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

Recent findings suggest that so how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Sources indicate that another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the Upcoming York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Sources indicate that another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

Industry observers note that arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross remarked no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!".

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand.".

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

Sources indicate that "People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!".

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

Industry observers note that micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 targets 30fps on both PS5 and PS5 Pro, but Digital Foundry’s first side-by-side comparison demonstrates a sharper image and steadier performance on Sony’s upgraded console.

Reviews for GTA 6 are in, and it’s already the joint best-reviewed game of all time, sitting right alongside Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

One outlet that has been incredibly impressed is video game tech analysis YouTube channel Digital Foundry, which has now given a deep dive into the differences between the base PS5 and PS5 Pro performance when it comes to playing GTA 6.

Digital Foundry’s John Linneman played GTA 6 for more than 50 hours on PS5 Pro without noticing a frame rate dip during normal gameplay. Well, besides a special case when he blew up multiple cars with a grenade launcher, which sent the Pro’s FPS down to 24 frames per second.

Linneman did note that this is a special case and the Pro frame rate stays smooth for the majority of gameplay, while the base PS5 indicated occasional drops during normal gameplay.

“They’re really very minor, but I noticed them, and it does slightly detract from the experience. It’s largely fine, and as I said earlier, it’s smoother than any GTA game at launch up till now, but I’d still like to have seen this cleaned up for release,” continued Linneman.

Industry observers note that the Pro also produces a noticeably clearer image, despite both versions appearing to render internally at 1440p. In its tech review, Linneman credits PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, or PSSR, for the Pro’s sharper presentation. He notes the technology reconstructs an image that “convincingly passes for native 4K,” while the standard PS5 more clearly resembles a 1440p image that has been upscaled.

GTA 6 running at 30 FPS “makes sense” experts say after Rockstar’s confirmation.

GTA 6 unlikely to be 60fps even on PS5 Pro according to experts.

PS5 Pro unlikely to run GTA 6 at 60 FPS – and that’s really sad actually.

“The difference in image quality is substantial,” says Linneman, with the comparison footage also showing more precise shadows on PS5 Pro. Both versions use ray-traced lighting and reflections, but the Pro adds ray-traced shadows that remove some of the rougher edges visible in the base PS5’s shadow maps.

The performance gap is less dramatic during ordinary play, though Linneman says the Pro delivers the definitive way to play GTA 6.

“I spent most of my time on the PS5 Pro, which is the best way to play this game by far. You basically get a near-flawless 30fps enhancement. The frame pacing is perfect, cutscenes are consistent and fluid, unlike older Rockstar titles, and everything moves without hiccups or stutters. It’s extremely solid, as you would hope, given that it’s only 30FPS.”.

Speaking to Wccftech, Rockstar’s developers also revealed that GTA 6 renders at 1440p on Xbox Series X before being upscaled to 4K using the studio’s own TAA solution, while the Xbox Series S version starts at 720p and uses AMD FSR Upscaling 4 to reach 1080p.

#408. SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

📅 19 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1429 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

📅 19 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1429 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine if one company could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy.
  • Among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers.
  • According to recent reports, the logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine if one company could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy. That potential fueled excitement around the long-anticipated initial public offering of SpaceX. Investors are not simply betting on rockets anymore. They are betting on an entire orbital ecosystem.

Among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers. SpaceX may be one of the most well-known companies seeking to build them, but it is not the only one.

According to recent reports, the logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints. As artificial intelligence drives an explosion in computing demand, companies are pitching orbital data centers as a way to escape the growing environmental and infrastructure pressures of Earth-based computing. Data centers often also face backlash from the public at having these centers located in their communities.

But there is a vast difference between launching satellites and operating an industrial-scale computing infrastructure in orbit. Space is unforgiving. Radiation damages electronics. The electronics generate enormous amounts of heat, and getting rid of that heat is surprisingly difficult in space. Repairs are extraordinarily expensive, and every pound rolled out into orbit still carries a significant cost.

We are engineering professors who study data center design and space systems engineering. Building a space-based data center will involve considerations from both sides.

First off, consider what goes into an Earth-based data center, like those that you’ve probably begun to see pop up everywhere. These facilities power cloud computing, video streaming, online banking, scientific computing and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. But a data center is much more than a room full of servers.

In a recent development, A data center needs several things to operate reliably. The first is electric power. Servers, networking equipment and storage devices consume large amounts of electricity, and that power demand is growing rapidly with AI.

The second is cooling. Almost all the electricity consumed by servers eventually becomes heat. If that heat is not removed swiftly and reliably, equipment performance drops, failures increase and the data center can shut down. Cooling systems often include air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps and, increasingly, liquid-cooling equipment. In many facilities, cooling is the largest energy consumer after the computing equipment itself.

It has been revealed that the third is physical infrastructure, including the necessary land, buildings, structural support, backup power, water systems, communication networks and maintenance access. Data centers also need to be close enough to people and network backbones to provide fast digital services.

In short, Earth-based data centers are large electrical and thermal infrastructure systems built around computing hardware.

So what would it take to build these data centers in space, and why are companies finding this possibility such an interesting business proposition?

As on Earth, these data centers would require massive amounts of power. In space, this power would come from solar panels. The Sun always shines in space and can’t be blocked by clouds. However, depending on the orbit the solar panels are put in, the Earth may shadow them for some portion of the orbit.

And even the best solar cells available today can convert only about half the sunlight that hits them to electricity.

Recent findings suggest that another potential advantage found in space is cooling. The cold background of space (near minus 455 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 270 degrees Celsius) creates an opportunity: waste heat from the data center could escape into space through radiators, keeping the electronics cool.

In a recent development, in principle, that design could eliminate some of the bulky and water-intensive cooling infrastructure used on Earth. However, those thermal radiators would require a large amount of surface area, and that would be in addition to the area required by the solar panels.

In space, there is no air to blow across hot equipment and help heat escape. The heat has to leave as infrared radiation, which is a relatively slow process. As a result, removing 10 megawatts of waste heat can require radiator surfaces comparable to the size of two football fields.

Recent findings suggest that space-based data centers could also avoid some of the local conflicts that come with building large data centers on the ground. Many communities resist new data center developments because of their land use, energy and water demand, and noise and environmental impact.

A space-based system would avoid competing for local land and water resources, and it would not generate neighborhood noise or require local zoning approval in the same way.

In a recent development, however, space is already getting crowded, and launching thousands of large orbital data centers would accelerate this concern. Orbital debris and micrometeorites are hazards because they can puncture the space data center, and a worst-case collision could destroy it and create even more space debris.

The frequency of space releases necessary to send all the equipment to orbit may also become a concern for some communities. SpaceX has had protests at its launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas, from local activists who argue that its rocket testing and launches damage the surrounding environment.

Recent findings suggest that all that data would need to be sent between Earth and these data centers – and between the data centers themselves – using radio waves or laser communications systems. Although satellite constellations such as Starlink and Amazon Leo have demonstrated that doing this is possible, the amount of data sent to and from space would balloon.

These data centers, along with their solar panels and radiators, cannot be released in one piece and would need to be assembled in space. This process would require newly introduced equipment for in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing.

In a recent development, another key challenge is the refresh cycle of computing hardware. Data center servers are not built to last forever. Operators on Earth usually replace or upgrade hardware every three to five years as chips improve, workloads change and equipment ages.

According to recent reports, and equipment failures can require replacing components. The refresh and repair processes are relatively straightforward on Earth, where workers can physically remove and replace servers.

In space, refresh and repair becomes much harder. Hardware sent to orbit may be difficult or too expensive to upgrade. If the computing platform cannot be updated, or too many components fail, it may become obsolete long before the surrounding infrastructure reaches the end of its useful life.

In a field where performance improves so rapidly and demand from computing continues to increase, this hurdle could prove a major economic and operational challenge.

It has been revealed that then there is the harshness of space. These data centers would be in a near vacuum, with constant radiation hitting them. And depending on their orbit, they would go from hot when in the sunlight to cold in Earth’s shadow many times a day. All of these challenges, and more, are complications that will need to be addressed.

It has been revealed that despite these challenges, companies are moving forward with designing space-based data centers. SpaceX just announced the design for its AI1 Compute Satellite, which it hopes to use as an orbital data center spacecraft. However, this satellite is 100 to 1,000 times less capable than current Earth-based data centers.

Not every computing task makes sense to do in space. Many data center applications depend on fast response times and close connections to consumers on Earth. Financial transactions, interactive AI services and most cloud applications are extremely sensitive to delay.

More feasible early applications may be those that are less latency-sensitive and more tightly connected to space operations. Examples could include processing Earth observation data from satellites, military or intelligence data processing, scientific computing related to space missions, or specialized computing for satellites and other space assets.

In other words, the first viable space data centers may serve space-based customers before they compete with mainstream cloud data centers on Earth.

Industry observers note that the world of augmented reality (AR) and extended reality (XR) glasses is really starting to get interesting. This is particularly true of so-called “self-contained” systems that don’t rely solely on your smartphone or tablet to deliver content. The Xreal Aura, which was co-developed with Google, is the latest in the Android XR field, and it’s quite an ambitious project.

In a recent development, although the Aura looks somewhat similar to previous Xreal glasses that we’ve reviewed, the AR goes a step further with a dedicated puck powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite SoC, hand/finger tracking, and the ability to interface wirelessly with accessories like keyboards and gamepads. The Aura really promises the ability to leave your smartphone at home and serve as the only computing platform you need (with some caveats).

The Aura’s design is clearly an evolution of the Xreal One Series, but with a few key differences. You’ll find the main changes up front, where you’ll now find two forward-facing, high-precision tracking cameras mounted at the corners of the frame. These cameras are used to continually track your head position, giving you the best possible experience for 6 degrees of freedom tracking for your hands and fingers.

At the center of the frame, there is a fully integrated single high-resolution camera for capturing photos or video. This was previously a separate add-on module for Xreal One Series AR glasses. There’s a red LED that illuminates when you’re recording so that people around you are made well aware of what’s going on if they have objections.

Industry observers note that your primary focal point, however, will be looking through the lenses, which are augmented by dual Sony-manufactured micro-OLED displays. You get one micro-OLED display per eye, each offering 1920 x 1200 resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and maximum brightness of 1,050 nits. However, there’s a major upgrade in the field of view (FoV), as the Aura expands to 70 degrees, up from 57 degrees on the One Pro.

According to recent reports, the Aura is available in two SKUs to support the interpupillary distance (IPD) of a wide range of people. The Medium SKU supports people with an IPD of 60 to 66 mm, while the Large SKU ranges from 66 mm to 72 mm.

Given that the Aura is the flagship of Xreal’s AR/XR glasses lineup, it comes with electrochromic dimming for the lenses, which can automatically adjust transparency levels, or you can manually make adjustments (there are five levels of transparency available).

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, the arms of the Aura look nearly identical to the ones you find on members of the One Series glasses. On the bottom is a red button, which, when pressed, allows you to manually adjust the brightness levels of the Aura. Directly adjacent is a rocker that allows you to control the volume. There’s another button on the top of the right arm that, when pressed once, takes you to the home menu. Double-pressing the button brings up the capture menu for taking pictures or videos with the forward-facing camera.

Bose-tuned speakers are also built into the arms of the Aura and feature an open-ear design so that you can remain engaged with what’s happening in your environment.

USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, Wi-Fi 6E, GPS.

Sources indicate that xreal takes a two-pronged approach to hardware with the Aura. At a base level, the Aura is powered by the X1S Spatial Coprocessor, which allows you to experience traditional AR functionality with smartphones, tablets, PCs, and Macs, as you would with previous Xreal glasses.

But the real magic happens with the Xreal Computing Puck, which is a separate device that connects to the Aura using a USB-C cable. The puck looks and feels like a slightly oversized smartphone, albeit without a display. In place of the display, you’ll find a large touch-sensitive surface that can be used to interface with the Android XR interface.

The puck is powered by Qualcomm’s fresh Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform, which delivers 48 TOPS of AI computing power. It comes in 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB SKUs — our review unit was spec’d with the former. The puck features a 4,455 mAh battery that powers the glasses, and it even incorporates a fingerprint reader for authentication purposes in Android XR. The puck also fully supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3; the latter of which is essential for supporting Bluetooth accessories.

The puck is quite beefy, measuring roughly 5.85 x 2.85 x 0.5 inches and weighing 9.3 ounces. I had no matter just slipping the puck into my pants pocket, but Xreal also includes a detachable clip if you want to attach it to your pants pocket or other clothing. The puck also features a cooling fan to keep temperatures in check. Indeed, the device can get warm to the touch (after all, it’s basically a powerful screenless smartphone with a 4,455 mAh battery) during use – which explains why Xreal includes the clip and probably doesn’t want you putting the puck in your pocket, like I was prone to do.

My Aura review unit also came with an Xreal Keyboard and an Xreal Game Controller. Both connect to the Aura using Bluetooth and were easily set up by pairing them within the Bluetooth menu under Settings.

Recent findings suggest that the keyboard is battery-powered and is recharged using a USB-C port at the top (just above the F7 key). It’s a nifty design that neatly folds when not in use. Interestingly, I couldn’t find a way to “lock” the hinged part of the keyboard when it’s fully extended. Because of this, you can’t use the keyboard sitting on your lap with your legs spread slightly apart, as the keyboard will simply collapse and fall to the floor if you apply any kind of pressure. You’ll either need to put your legs together or place the keyboard on a desk or table, which isn’t exactly ideal if you like the more “freeing” aspect of using XR glasses.

In a recent development, with that noted, the keyboard is a lifesaver when it comes to text entry, be it for entering web addresses, writing emails, or anything that requires frequent use of the keyboard. It sure beats waving your fingers around to input text.

The game controller features an Xbox-style layout with four face buttons for gaming, two thumbsticks, a D-pad, and a Google Gemini/Home button. There are two shoulder buttons at the top and two triggers (with modes to function as microswitch triggers or Hall Effect analog triggers). There are also two remappable macro buttons under the shoulder buttons and two additional macro buttons on the underside of the controller (which can be turned off with physical switches).

Sources indicate that not only does the controller feature built-in rumble, but it also incorporates a 6-axis gyroscope for aiming and finger controls and a 3.5mm headphone jack built into the bottom of the unit. But perhaps the most interesting feature is a magnetic faceplate that breaks into three pieces. The main piece covers the face buttons, D-pad, and thumbsticks. The other two pieces cover the hand grips. You can purchase separate pieces to customize the look of the controller if you wish.

I found the controller comfortable to use, with a nice textured plastic finish for your palms to rest on (the bottom of the controller features a similar texture, but has a rubber coating over the plastic for better grip). And although the controller is designed for Bluetooth use with the Aura, it does feature a USB-C port and a USB dongle for connecting it wirelessly to a PC.

Another nice touch is that Xreal includes a charging dock for the controller that plugs in with a lengthy USB-A to USB-C cable. The controller itself charges with four pogo pins mounted on top of the dock (or via USB-C if you prefer).

After removing the Aura from its retail box, I wanted to get into the action rapidly and didn’t bother initially charging the puck. I used the included USB-C to USB-C cable to plug from the left arm of the Aura into the dedicated USB-C port on the bottom of the puck. Next, I pressed the power button on the puck, after which the glasses sprang to life and began the setup process.

After taking some time to get used to dragging and pinching through the Android XR interface using my fingers, the experience began to feel almost natural. I was able to pinch to open apps, have multiple apps open at once, and drag or resize windows in my viewing space on command.

Industry observers note that I was able to access all the typical stock apps like Chrome, Gmail, and Google Photos, which, of course, carried over my favorites, emails, and photos/vidoes, respectively. I spent quite a bit of time going down memory lane, watching videos of my two sons when they were toddlers among the hundreds of videos I have stored in Google Photos. It was also great to be navigating around the UI or working in the app, then seeing a notification pop up telling me that an email had arrived. I would then pinch the notification with my fingers to open Gmail.

According to recent reports, the possibilities of how you can use the Aura are almost endless, and you can even mix other computing devices into the formula. For example, I was able to plug a USB-C cable from my MacBook Air into the second USB-C port on the puck (that’s usually reserved for recharging the puck). In an instant, my MacBook Air’s display was mirrored onto the glasses in front of me. So I could have Google Docs open as I typed, while having the Android XR native Gmail and YouTube apps flanking the virtual MacBook Air display.

It’s a similar experience with handheld gaming consoles. I was successfully able to connect a Lenovo Legion Go S (SteamOS) and an MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Windows 11) to the Aura glasses without issue, enjoying a vast library of games in fully immersive glory.

The native gaming experience isn’t bad either; I loaded up games like Fortnite and spent an hour toiling around in Grand Theft Auto III for a nostalgic treat ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The Xreal Game Controller made playing these games a breeze.

But I also used the Aura glasses for more mundane tasks. I was able to walk around the house, performing my usual chores, with a shrunken YouTube window playing videos in the top right corner of my field of view. True multitasking is at hand, folks.

Recent findings suggest that I should note that open-air speakers sounded good, but not great. They sounded similar to the Bose-tuned speakers in the older Xreal One Pro. There's a good level of bass, and overall clarity is good. However, if you want a more immersive audio experience, the design of the Aura allows you to easily throw on a pair of headphones or wireless earbuds to compensate for any audio shortcomings.

The Xrea Aura is a true workhorse when it comes to spatial computing. By putting the bulk of the computing hardware into a smartphone-shaped Computing Puck, you have a low-impact way of experiencing XR without the hassle of wearing a bulky headset.

In a recent development, you can navigate the user interface using your hands, or the touch service of the puck. And for more specialized tasks, Xreal offers its own-branded keyboard and gamepad accessories (although you are free to use your own Bluetooth-enabled accessories).

Not only do you have access to the vast Android app ecosystem, but you can also connect to devices running Windows, macOS, or even SteamOS.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot going on with this device, and there are limitless possibilities for how you could use the Aura. The only problem is that most people don’t have limitless funds, so the $1,099 price tag of our review unit (12GB RAM, 256GB of storage) is sure to give many people pause. Stepping up to 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage takes the price to $1,299. If you add in the Xreal Keyboard and Xreal Game Controller, the total cost of our review unit comes in at $1,277 ($1,477 for the 16GB/512GB configuration).

That’s a lot to ask for what is essentially a niche device. However, if you want a truly immersive XR experience that is not weighed down by geeky-looking headsets, it’s hard to argue with what Xreal is offering with the Aura.

When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight (Nov. 17-18) sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

According to recent reports, up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell.

According to recent reports, leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere. By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors.

Recent findings suggest that shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark.

As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors, which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.

The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

Read more: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966.

According to recent reports, sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society, another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034.

Industry observers note that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1, with an Nvidia lawyer following him on December 2, it's been confirmed. CNBC reports that the leaders of those panels broke the news today after days of speculation. Huang was asked to appear via a letter issued on November 9, just 24 hours after he admitted the affair with Alice Huang, a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy. Days later, it was also suggested that Mr. Huang could be issued a subpoena if he did not respond by tomorrow, November 18. That subpoena will no longer be required.

Sources indicate that “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Rick Crawford, R-Ark., the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees, reportedly said after the news of the pair's December appearances was announced. "The American people need answers," they went on, noting that it would be "dangerous" to allow Chinese state actors access to advanced AI chips, the likes of which are built by Nvidia.

Ms. Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a organization that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr. Huang's tenure as CEO. Megaspeed was later added to Nvidia's no-sell list following concerns that it was involved in the smuggling of AI chips to China against U.S. export laws. Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary, has been accused of importing Nvidia chips and then re-exporting them to China. A criminal investigation has since been launched into Megaspeed in an attempt to get to the bottom of the complicated web of AI companies and chip shipments.

According to recent reports, jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia following his admission of an affair with Ms. Huang. Since then, reports of at least one other affair with an Nvidia employee have surfaced. Despite that fact, calls for Huang's return to the top job at Nvidia continue to gain momentum.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games has laid off around 60 people.

The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving.

According to recent reports, its sources say Firaxis' unannounced XCOM game has faced development struggles and missed "a significant milestone over the summer". The project will continue, but "may face a shakeup as a result of the cuts".

A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two label that runs Firaxis, confirmed Hazen's departure to Bloomberg, and noted the studio is "restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years".

According to recent reports, "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis," the spokesperson continued. "These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.".

The layoffs come two days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is developed and published by Rockstar, a separate label at Take-Two.

Industry observers note that in September, around 18 months after Civ 7's widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - Firaxis unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game as it continued to improve it. These included an atomic age enhancement, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick admitted earlier this year that the studio "got it wrong with Civ 7".

"The game is a really good game. And it's certainly a profitable enterprise for us. But this is one where I think what we tried to do was a bridge too far, from the consumer's perspective," he told Game File in May.

It’s not the first round of cuts at the studio - 2K confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs at Firaxis in September 2025, and around 30 jobs went in 2023.

#402. Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

📅 29 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)
