💡 Key Takeaways
  • STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.
  • Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov.
  • It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX indicates is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite rolls out worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

Industry observers note that it hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet noted whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has for years been happy to let this practice continue on its platform, and as such a sort of cultural norm about hopping on a digital plane for a game's release has been established. According to the Wall Street Journal, an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China.

Recent findings suggest that the open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, they did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico.
  • In a recent development, it also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

In a recent development, they did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

In a recent development, it also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

It has been revealed that "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's.".

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

Sources indicate that the Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#379. Newly introduced programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)

Newly introduced programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
  • The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
  • Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how rapidly they can transmit data.

Industry observers note that these challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

Industry observers note that however, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait.

Industry observers note that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information swiftly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

According to recent reports, systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility.

It has been revealed that traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

According to recent reports, that lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever upcoming capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light.

Industry observers note that the research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a fresh design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Sources indicate that using the latest CRIT structure, the researchers demonstrated that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape.

In a recent development, the researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also indicated that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical.

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions.

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several crucial capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers.

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Strategy Larger Programmable Photonic Systems.

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a latest design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We proposal to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.".

Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We blueprint to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.".

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

According to recent reports, dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

In a recent development, materials provided by Seoul National University College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A free Christian parody of Grand Theft Auto is launching alongside GTA 6, and getting five stars will bring Satan after you instead of the cops.

With players finally jumping into Vice City, satire site The Babylon Bee is opening up a city of its own. The game is called Grand Faith Auto, and it takes place in Upcoming Mercy, a 3D open world you can explore right in your browser.

The setup will look familiar to anyone who’s played GTA, as there are cars to take, storefronts and billboards dotted around the city, and a radar to help you find your way.

But while the real thing often throws you into the criminal underworld, Grand Faith Auto is all about being an upstanding citizen.

Instead of the traditional Wanted level, doing good deeds earns you stars of divine approval. Get all five, and the devil himself comes looking for you instead of the cops.

One of the deeds you can do around Newly introduced Mercy is pull a driver out of their car and preach to them before driving off in it yourself. You can also offer a “Lady of the Night” a lift to church, or try to feed the hungry in a scenario involving a closed chicken restaurant, a deli under attack, and a box of pocket Bibles.

There’s even a stealth mission where you sneak into a cartel warehouse and swap its drugs for little figurines. You’ll have to stay out of sight, because getting spotted by a guard is an instant fail.

The official Grand Faith Auto game launch trailer. It's the upcoming hit video game everyone's been waiting to play for years. Available November 18!Grand Faith Auto is free, while Grand Theft Auto VI will cost your eternal soul (plus $80).Just go to https://t.co/21fFFTXowv pic.twitter.com/aBJRRtTeZY.

Industry observers note that you’re not completely unarmed, though, as you can wield a holy shotgun to fend off the imps tracking you down. A shot to the head stuns them, leaving you free to kick them back to hell. After that, the instructions tell you to go to church.

Police can’t wait for GTA 6 to be released so they can “catch a break”.

GTA 6 forces you to take your time with the main story instead of speedrunning it.

GTA 6 best guides for launch: Everything you need to know.

Discussing the game in an X post, The Baylon Bee CEO Seth Dillon mentioned that he doesn’t expect the game to actually rival GTA 6, it’s just a “Christian alternative.”.

That’s probably for the best, given that GTA 6 has already become the joint-best-reviewed game of all time.

#377. Latest Update: Grand Theft Auto 6 review

Latest Update: Grand Theft Auto 6 review

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, my best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely.
  • I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's.
  • Recent findings suggest that I could go on about this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, my best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they mentioned, paraphrasing, have found a fresh 'third place': the car.

I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly massive and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without.

Recent findings suggest that I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5, its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't.

According to recent reports, reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape.

I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x'. To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.

Recent findings suggest that whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about massive ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.

It has been revealed that none of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything.

GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms.

Sources indicate that jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes.

What else can be noted? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things.

Recent findings suggest that the fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.

Sources indicate that buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those latest wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list.

Pick up some groceries. Get those flowers. Grab some clothes for Lucia to change into. Maybe finish those odd DIY jobs you've left half-started around the place so, y'know, your bedroom actually has a wall. Ever since GTA 4, and Roman Bellic's slightly desperate calls to go play darts and shoot some pool, Rockstar has leant further and further into the mundane. But here the studio has gone many steps further, past the Sopranos of GTA 5 and poker of Red Dead Redemption 2, full-tilt into slice-of-life. The result, mercifully, is anything but dull - all these situations, familiar as they may be, are really moments for irony, humour, character, just as they are in life itself. That, and a welcome chance to catch your breath amidst the bombast, which accelerates from these early missions exponentially.

That early, to-do list mission is like a lot of other moments in GTA, in that it's a case of Rockstar not-so-subtly dropping hints. This time, it's "we are going to play with your priorities". If there's a constant in GTA 6, you realise, it's that there often seems to be a nagging thought in the back of your mind as you progress. Should I be prioritising this right now? Is that optional thing worth the effort? Will this choice matter? How? It's such a prominent thought as you play, the actual act of devising what systems this game is using as you progress is as interesting in itself as how those systems end up working. Or to put it more simply: figuring this game out for yourself is really part of the fun.

It has been revealed that back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later).

Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff).

And those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the significant, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else.

It has been revealed that small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV indicates, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating.

It has been revealed that none of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond.

All together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played.

It has been revealed that I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States.

It has been revealed that I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely newly introduced when I drive through them again.

At one point, amongst the forest of the national park up in Leonida's northern third - trundling down one winding dirt track among many, trees in all directions - I actually found myself slightly lost. At least for a moment, anyway, until I plonked down a map marker and the GPS sorted me out. GTA 6 asks more of you than any previous GTA game, but it's also a retraction from the intentional clunk of Red Dead Redemption 2. You'll never be truly stuck or stumped; there's no sense of toil.

A quick example: the Scooter Bros (remember those?!) return here in a delightful reference, now acting as an official in-game phone app that lets you summon an owned vehicle for a fee, or up to three times a day if you unlock the app's "unlimited" version for a one-off cost. They can also repair your car or recover it if, like me, you have a habit of landing it on its roof. You can also fix it up at the returning Pay 'n' Spray's and all-upcoming gas stations - which, thankfully, you really don't need to visit for refuelling all that often. (When you do, it's often worth the time: this is a great window for an emergent event to pop up - more on those, too, later.).

Recent findings suggest that soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself.

Time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning aims for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe.

I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles, and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall.

According to recent reports, this is not a patch of paint designed to be noticed. It's in the foreground for a fraction of a second as Lucia heads into another room, but it stuck for precisely that reason. This is the product of someone looking intensely at the environment as they attempt to recreate it and realising how key imperfections are to simulating reality. Clearly someone's scuffed, scratched, or graffitied something outside of this office, and the penitentiary system has felt the need to paint over it in some vain declaration of order. And then tight budgets, like a crumbling English council once again repainting a playground fence, have dictated the colour of paint that'll be used - likely whatever was to hand - to cover up these little marks of rebellion.

Industry observers note that I looked at this and wrote it down. And then a few hours later, as I was whizzing around this world evading cop cars, hopping out to make a mad dash for cover, I realised how pointless that was. I'd already been darting by piles and piles of this stuff. Back alleys filled with rubbish - glorious rubbish, the most decadent scrap metal, buckets of mulch, and sacks of rotting food waste you've ever seen - and tables covered in piles of tat. Back offices stacked with papers, posters, family photos, files, mugs, notices, trophies, pens, and all kinds of amalgamated bric-a-brac that forms a picture of a real office in the mind.

The point is: at first, as Rockstar gently guides you from place to place, gradually layering the systems onto one another, easing you into this ocean of water by toe, ankle, knee, waist, you think it's doing that thing where video games front load fidelity to set the tone, maybe flex a little, before easing up after hitting you with some big and glorious view. Then you realise this is just what this game is like. It's everywhere. A huge amount of this map is, in the nicest possible way, kind of pointless. It's things - a disused motel, a lumber mill - which have no mission or character attached, and are instead there predominantly because in a real world they would be there, and therefore, to Rockstar, they must be there.

Industry observers note that in some moments, if you're like me, it might genuinely create a kind of sadness: the sheer, incomprehensible amount of things that have evidently been slaved over by literally thousands of humans (some of whom, notably, currently locked in an employment tribunal with Rockstar over alleged union-busting) that will almost certainly be missed. Things you'll fly by in an instant as you whip the camera round the room in search of valuables or escape routes, never to return, worker hours piling up like grains of sand on Vice City's heavenly beach. It's so easy to focus on breadth and scale when talking about GTA 6's world. The volume. The "content". But what matters more I think is this miniscule detail. There's a point where detail, in a simulated world, tips over into effective infinity, where your brain just learns to let it glide on by. A point I never thought an open world game could ever truly reach - and yet here we are. In turn it creates almost a kind of obligation to linger - linger, that is, in a game built to be experienced from behind the wheel of a supercar. Another point of brilliant tension.

Speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself.

It has been revealed that and the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against.

According to recent reports, over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a upcoming-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft.

Sources indicate that theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this big metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will.

This is where a lot of the various systems teased in previews - all of which sounded, on the surface, kind of awkward to me - weave into what the game is trying to do. There are several here, all overlapping in their own way and typically evolving - but not outright replicating - ideas first brought in via Read Dead Redemption 2. The combined impact is a sense of constant decision-making, tension once again between the immediacy of steaming in somewhere and tearing away from the cops, and the satisfaction of a slightly more restrained proposal.

Sources indicate that to stick with money, it operates in a kind of tiered system. At the bottom you have cash, which has a $20,000 limit per character and which can be lost in its entirety, particularly when you're wasted or busted. Once you've unlocked your BuckMe (yep) account - a kind of PayPal parody - cash can be deposited at ATMs into a much safer kind of basic shared current account. Even that is at risk of charges of some kind when you're killed or arrested - I've yet to reverse engineer what dictates these, but they're at worse in the low thousands, typically less. Then above that is your savings account, again shared across Jason and Lucia, where your money is at its safest but also, crucially, irretrievable once deposited.

In a recent development, the physical act of collecting money is now an action, too, as opposed to something you can simply run over and vacuum up. You need to manually collect it from characters' bodies, from the counter after being placed there by a panicked cashier, from inside safes you crack, and so on. Sometimes it might be in a locked container - such as when you bust open an ATM - which you'll need to shoot first to access. Sometimes it's stored behind a bank's vault door, which only opens in a very specific circumstance, meaning a narrow, heist-like window needs to be exploited in order for it to be reached. And when you're stealing anything other than clean cash - namely jewellery, marked bills, and drugs - you'll store it in a stash bag.

That feeds into two other systems here, which both operate around a sense of ownership, in vehicles and weapons. Stash bags contain all your loot until they're filled, and then they need to be sold to a fence - with different fences offering more or less for certain goods, or not taking some at all - before you can actually access the profit. You can drop these bags when you're hit by a car or knocked off a bike (or, ahem, fumbling with the controls for a second), and likewise hand them off to your partner to carry or even independently sell for you. You can also store them in your car's trunk, where they're slightly safer, but also then take slightly longer to access if, say, you're switching vehicles mid four-star cop chase along the freeway.

It has been revealed that and cars and weapons also follow a similar system in turn: stolen cars are now only temporarily yours; safe when stored in a parking spot but at risk when out in the world, until you pay to register them with a fence (or, later in the game, at Pay 'n' Sprays). But owned cars are yours forever, even when destroyed, as long as you have enough garage space to store them - garage space that, you realise, costs more and more money to procure. The same goes for weapons: found weapons are essentially borrowed, and lost when you're killed or arrested. But owned weapons - ones you buy, or unique, custom ones you discover - are yours forever, recoverable even if lost or left behind.

It has been revealed that this then, in turn, ties into the upcoming police and 'wanted' system. Now it's much more realistic: police can spot or receive reports of you and take note of several factors, from facial appearance to clothing, whether you're with your partner, what weapon you have on you and what vehicle you're driving. And when it comes to things like robbing stores and banks, there's a system for whether you're spotted on locally stored CCTV, which can be destroyed, or fancier cloud-based footage which can't.

All kinds of things then play into this, from whether you walk into a place with a "longarm" gun - automatically putting guards on high alert - or a concealed pistol, to whether you're committing a crime somewhere fancy or rough. I got a strong sense that my crimes were being far less attentively dealt with in Vice City's poorer neighbourhoods. There are also two rings of attention drawn on the map when you're wanted, dictating how intensely a police search for you is concentrated, and different kinds of star ratings too, via a system called heat. These indicate whether police can see you, have a description of you, or are simply looking for a criminal for the crime you performed in that area. Even after you successfully escape, heat - dictated by whatever police might know - remains over the entire region of your crime, the size of that area and rate of its deterioration depending on just what exactly that crime was.

In a recent development, finally, the criminal profile system is another tangent on its own, but once again it all folds together. It's a tiered honour system ranking you from "Professional" at one end to "Irredeemable" at the other, that last one the only point from which your reputation can never be recovered. Incapacitations instead of kills - which crucially are satisfying and easy to achieve with a bit of concentration - as well as completing objectives more subtly or achieving cleaner getaways from crimes, will tilt you towards Pro status. Driving that tank over those civilians or, heaven forbid, kicking a dog takes you the other way. If this sounds burdensome, again I'd say you really shouldn't worry: I naturally found myself with both Jason and Lucia as Professionals at the end, mostly thanks to shooting lots of cops in the groin. Your necessary actions during missions or when under attack don't impact it in the same way, I gather. It feels closer to a case of illustrating the role play on offer here, and ultimately committing to the consequences of that, than it does any kind of struggle to manage.

All in all, the effect with the overall game is similar: less that GTA 6 becomes hard work - as I'd feared myself, and as Rockstar intentionally made Red Dead Redemption 2, to its thematic benefit in many ways - and more that, now, a greater amount of what you're doing is gamified. A robbery is in itself a game: whether you go in loud or quiet, together or separate, or focus on cracking the safe or looting the registers. As is how you divide up the bags between you, or whether your getaway is done together or separately to split cops' attention; whether you use your own car or a stolen vehicle, and if you're smart enough to park another one somewhere out of sight nearby for a sneaky changeover. You can also pack changes of clothes in your car to help disguise your identity.

And all that's introduced, ingeniously, via the main missions of Jason and Lucia's story. If you were ever in doubt that GTA might have lost its edge, amongst all these soft and cuddly themes and grand ideas - that it might be sacrificed at the altar of realism and narrative heft - you can put that worry firmly aside. The low-brow humour, parody, larger-than-life characters, out of body experiences, 90s film references or cops-n-robbers bombast are all here, and all about as good as they've ever been.

In fact, really, in a lot of cases they're quite a bit better. The highlights are hard to pick out without spoiling again - many of the best arise from moments where you wonder if the game will go there, before it inevitably does. Others involve movie references that feel more overt than ever - Lucia openly quotes John McClane at one point, lighter in hand - but while some of this can feel a tad predictable, the sheer spectacle is often spellbinding.

The best moments, aptly, come in car chases, where tyres are eviscerated by gunfire and speeding 4x4s suddenly dip, flip, and crash into one another with a sensational boom. Clearly some magic has been worked under the hood here to ensure that when they crash out, they do so with a kind of cinematic, organic-looking stuntman style, swerving into other vehicles in the chasing pack, across lanes into trucks and lorries, over highway partitions, wrapping around trees or catapulting off bridges. The newly introduced focus system - bullet time, on a specific, buffable meter - highlights weak spots such as engines and tyres for you to aim at for generally non-lethal take-outs, helping you with yet another system I'll get to in a moment. But really that system is kind of secondary here: I started shooting at these spots because, more often than not, it rewarded me with something awesome.

According to recent reports, main missions and the bigger character-based, optional side missions work similarly to how they've done before in GTA games. A location is marked on a map and you head there, or call someone, or wait for a call, and once you arrive things kick off, elements of the open world closing somewhat as self-contained scenarios within the sandbox open up. There are few low points, as the first act glides through a wistfully carefree, low-key criminal life before the game shifts to the snowballing momentum of its crooks-on-the-run melodrama. There are multiple heists, which are naturally high watermarks - significant moments of catharsis and chaos that propel the couple forward across some new Rubicon after hours and hours of sub-mission preparations. There are episodes with every vehicle, every ludicrous modern American scenario, every body part you could imagine. You'll be dragged through all kinds of Floridian subcultures, naturally, from sleepy key life and everglades hicks to rusted-over rural towns, biker gangs, strip clubs, record labels, towerblock drug kingpins and, erm, bodybuilders. And then plenty beyond that.

Rockstar is as ever ruthless with the skewer. The targets remain broad, from Miami's upcoming wave of non-indigenous crypto bros to wellness Bali girlies aiming to be their very own #SheEO. But there's also a maturity here, believe it or not, even if it's slightly tucked away between the dangling wangs and murderous– actually I won't spoil that one. I've found no cases of Rockstar punching down - although rest assured no progressive, gentrifying hipster goes unscathed - and there is a subtle, but absolutely present awareness of the world in which Rockstar is now operating. In one moment the concept of using dirt on a senator is discussed, at which point Jason wisely remarks that dirt must be pretty spectacular, given what they've already gotten away with these days.

According to recent reports, the changes here are small, ultimately, and while there's a whole essay of its own to be written about the concept of parody, my sense is Rockstar has played this just right. GTA 6 has essentially taken the 'mirror' approach, in simply concentrating the extremes of the current world - so often deemed impervious to satire - by putting them all together in a single place, then reflecting them back at the world they came from. Florida is often described as a kind of heightened America - America Plus, the country's Ultimate Edition - and Leonida is just a heightened Florida. With an awful lot of very silly puns.

Recent findings suggest that away from the main missions and primary sidequests, Rockstar's made another seemingly subtle, but kind of revolutionary tweak. Aside from more static activities - the races, sports, pastimes, and the rest - the other source of missions in GTA 6 is what the game calls emergent events. These are entirely missable - though I think they re-present themselves eventually - and occur essentially as overheard goings-on just out of shot. They could be anything from one-off opportunities or minor punchlines to entire quest chains and conspiracies.

In a recent development, for instance: driving around Vice City you might find a guy doing his best Florida Man impression by livestreaming himself to his Snapmatic following while standing on the highway overpass wall above a high drop. Then, inevitably, he slips and you might be able to pull him up or might - as I may or may not have done - fumble the controls and have him plummet to his death. You might watch a bunch of amateurs rob a payday loans store and get blasted by the marked bills' exploding dye. Or a group of masked, heavily-armed professionals rob a cash truck or minor bank. A weirdo might flag you down and trigger a whole load of nonsense happening next, or the cops might be arresting someone and leave a supercar and bag of coke happily unattended while they try to run off. Even beyond that, there's also just weird stuff lying around, without anything specific tied to it. I once spent a worrying amount of time in conversation with a pioneering member of the Hollow Earth Society. Then got a good laugh when I next paid him a visit.

It has been revealed that it's a cracking system, in part because it reinforces a sense of continuous, organic weirdness around every corner, and in part because each of these feels like a kind of invitation. Once you do a couple and find yourself blackmailing a guy who in turn blackmailed GTA's in-game Amazon equivalent for a cut of his lawsuit winnings, or spraying manure on a spurned farmer's ex-lover's house, or running over some numpty protesters trying to set an actual bear loose on the freeway, it's hard not to stop at every distant argument or out-of-pocket comment that crosses your airwaves. Rest assured, if you think I've spoiled anything here: there are scores of these events, many of which I've yet to encounter or investigate, and many of which are far weirder and more curious than these.

All this feeds back into a sense of choice, which is a challenge to accurately describe, thanks to both how difficult it is to figure out when and how one might have mattered, and when a moment of the story might have diverged. But choices, combined with the strength of your relationship and your criminal profile, and other factors I'll intentionally decline to mention here, all have an impact. One particularly great achievement of Rockstar's, in fact, is in making you wrestle with those choices, within missions and without, in this state of blindness to their outcomes. Even whether they're significant at all is often unknown - in many cases the variables, permutations and forks are still unknown to me now, after all this time - and yet also, once again without spoiling any moment at any point, the studio has still made whatever outcomes you might encounter feel as resonant as any I've experienced. Forgive me for dodging any examples and insisting you take my word for it.

Away from missions themselves, of which there are of course many, and there are so many more things to do beyond them. You can dive for treasure across dozens of underwater sites. You can bird watch, animal watch, fish, and hunt for game. You can customise guns and cars to extreme ends - please do the street racing side missions for a, ahem, lovely example of custom wrapping - and customise your characters just as much. The fitness system is great, with a surprising number of superbly animated gym and bodyweight exercises and, naturally, walking BBLs who hit on Jason as he demonstrates perfect form.

According to recent reports, it's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too.

According to recent reports, there's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk reveals and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game.

Recent findings suggest that the overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the significant financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else.

It has been revealed that what you realise is you're pairing all this stuff to do - ultimately, variations on simply hanging out - with the fact that so much of Jason and Lucia's relationship is delivered in quiet, hang-out moments. And as so many of their other relationships - with parents, adopted parents, friends - come in the same way, this picture starts to form. From an apartment sofa to the Vice Beach waves, GTA 6 is ultimately just a place to be.

In fact, in many ways it's a kind of evolution of the hangout game itself. The gentle, wistful, nostalgic guitar strums from Justice's background score as you idle on the map or menu. The dedication, through all those years of what I imagine to be Rockstar's incessant tinkering with sounds and performances and tiny visual touches, to an authentic sense of place. I could melt into this world. I think about the amount of people about to play this game, and the way it invites you to submerge yourself in it like a hot bath, and wonder if the axis of the entire hangout genre - maybe the biggest paradigm shift in video games of the last two decades - might have suddenly been shifted again. The comfort of continuously mic'd up pal chatter replaced here with a kind of sublime isolation.

It has been revealed that there are, as I mentioned, a few very little flaws I could pick at. Some of the missions for Dre-Quan, a record label-owning friend of Jason involving a newly invented rap group for the game, were fun in their own right, extraordinarily well produced and an essential part of the whole, but also just a little throwaway in a sense. There seemed to be little tie-in from those to the progress of the actual story, leaving them feeling a little more like lavish side missions than a part of the main event, contributing to a little mid-game narrative sag. The controls, while a marked improvement from Red Dead Redemption 2 - I fear I'll never make it to heaven after the amount of times I accidentally punched that horse - could still be tighter. Shooting is less wafty than it has been for some time, forgoing auto-aim for aim-assist (though settings can be heavily tinkered or restored to those of GTA 5), and GTA is now a proper third-person cover shooter in its action moments, with better snapping to cover and dashing between it, which suits it perfectly. But there were still moments where the controls wobbled. Walking three steps along a narrow beam to open a small container without falling off felt like the hardest thing the game asked me to do in its entire runtime.

According to recent reports, what else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier.

I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro, but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering.

Recent findings suggest that A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine.

And this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of New York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

It has been revealed that what is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I mentioned it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every big score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.

A copy of Grand Theft Auto 6 was provided for this review by Rockstar.
